exploreAction.targetName: Oblomov, the opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Oblomov, where the hero stays on his sofa through every visitor's appeal. Notice how Goncharov makes inaction hilarious and strangely moving. Write what Oblomov's refusal means — laziness, protest, or fear?

name: Varlam Shalamov
teaser: The Russian writer who survived seventeen years in the Kolyma labor camps and spent his life writing Kolyma Tales — short, unsparing stories that refuse all comfort and nearly all metaphor.

exploreAction.targetName: Kolyma Tales, a short story
exploreAction.instruction: Read one story from Kolyma Tales. Notice how Shalamov reports the camps without sentiment — frostbite, bread, the logic of survival. Write why he said prose must be 'cold' and what that coldness preserves.

name: Mikhail Sholokhov
teaser: The Cossack novelist of And Quiet Flows the Don — an epic of revolution told through one family's river of blood and love. He won the Nobel and remains Russia's most monumental storyteller of the civil war.

exploreAction.targetName: And Quiet Flows the Don, opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of the epic, where the river and the village are introduced through the Melekhov family. Notice how Sholokhov grounds vast history in one household. Write how the Don itself becomes a character.

name: Andrey Bely
teaser: The Russian symbolist whose novel Petersburg is a prose symphony of the city — a cubist, ticking, hallucinated Petersburg on the eve of revolution. Nabokov ranked it among the greatest novels of the century.

exploreAction.targetName: Petersburg, the opening pages
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Petersburg. Notice how the city is described in fragments, rhythms, and strange geometries. Write how the prose itself performs the nervous energy of the revolution it narrates.

name: Sławomir Mrożek
teaser: The Polish playwright and cartoonist of the absurd. His short stories and dramas, like Tango, use surreal logic to expose totalitarian habits — funny, bleak, and devastatingly precise.

exploreAction.targetName: Mrożek's short stories, a selection
exploreAction.instruction: Read three of Mrożek's very short stories. Notice how each begins with a plausible situation that tilts into the absurd. Write how comedy becomes a way of telling the truth about power that plain description cannot reach.

name: Aleksandar Hemon
teaser: The Bosnian-American novelist stranded in Chicago by the siege of Sarajevo, who learned English and wrote The Question of Bruno and The Lazarus Project — memory, displacement, and history braided together.

exploreAction.targetName: The Question of Bruno, a story
exploreAction.instruction: Read a story from The Question of Bruno. Notice how Hemon scrambles chronology, genre, and voice. Write how the experience of exile shapes a writer's relationship to language — what does it mean to be 'born again' into English?

name: Andrey Kurkov
teaser: The Ukrainian novelist of the absurd and the everyday — Death and the Penguin follows a writer who keeps a penguin named Misha in post-Soviet Kyiv. His books read like black comedies of survival.

exploreAction.targetName: Death and the Penguin, opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Death and the Penguin. Notice how Viktor's life — obituaries for the living, a penguin for company — is both surreal and perfectly believable. Write how the penguin becomes a mirror of its owner's isolation.

name: Serhiy Zhadan
teaser: The Ukrainian poet and novelist of the east — Kharkiv's chronicler. Voroshilovgrad and The Orphanage mix punk energy, tenderness, and war; his poetry speaks for a generation living through upheaval.

exploreAction.targetName: The Orphanage, opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of The Orphanage. Notice how Zhadan balances the surreal violence of war with precise domestic detail. Write how the novel treats the duty to protect one child while the world burns around you.

name: Mikhail Saltykov-Shchedrin
teaser: The great Russian satirist of the 19th century, whose The Golovlyov Family and The History of a Town flayed bureaucracy, serfdom, and hypocrisy with savage laughter. Dostoevsky called him a prophet.

exploreAction.targetName: The Golovlyov Family, opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of The Golovlyov Family. Notice how Saltykov-Shchedrin's portrait of a decaying gentry family mixes farce and horror. Write how the novel's central figure, Iudushka, becomes a study in sanctimonious cruelty.

name: Henrik Ibsen
teaser: The Norwegian playwright who made the modern drama — A Doll's House, Hedda Gabler, and Ghosts ripped open the respectable home and let the 19th century's lies out. Every argument play owes him a debt.

exploreAction.targetName: A Doll's House, Act One
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first act of A Doll's House. Notice how Nora performs her little-bird role while secretly managing a huge debt. Write how Ibsen plants the crisis in the first scene, and what the 'doll's house' metaphor contains.

name: Hans Christian Andersen
teaser: The Danish storyteller whose fairy tales — The Little Mermaid, The Ugly Duckling, The Snow Queen — are darker, stranger, and more honest than their Disney versions. He wrote about longing and being an outsider.

exploreAction.targetName: The Little Mermaid, the original tale
exploreAction.instruction: Read the original Little Mermaid. Notice how different it is from the cartoon — pain, sacrifice, and an ending about souls rather than weddings. Write what the tale really says about love, transformation, and loss.

name: Karen Blixen
teaser: The Danish baroness who wrote as Isak Dinesen — author of Out of Africa and Seven Gothic Tales. Her ornate, ironic, storytelling-rich prose made her one of the 20th century's most distinctive voices.

exploreAction.targetName: Babette's Feast
exploreAction.instruction: Read Babette's Feast. Notice how Blixen builds a whole theology of generosity around a French cook and a puritan village. Write what the dinner means as a work of art — and what the story says about giving everything.

name: Sigrid Undset
teaser: The Norwegian Nobel laureate whose medieval epic Kristin Lavransdatter follows one woman's fierce life across marriage, faith, and motherhood in 14th-century Norway. Few novels render a soul so completely.

exploreAction.targetName: Kristin Lavransdatter, The Wreath, opening
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of The Wreath. Notice how Undset immerses you in medieval Norwegian domestic life — food, cloth, weather — without costume-pageant decoration. Write how the historical setting deepens rather than decorates the love story.

name: Tarjei Vesaas
teaser: The Norwegian master of the spare, the elemental. The Ice Palace is a short novel about two girls and an ice formation that is one of the most haunting books ever written in any language.

exploreAction.targetName: The Ice Palace, opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of The Ice Palace. Notice how Vesaas writes in short, precise sentences that feel translated from snow and silence. Write how the frozen waterfall becomes both a real place and a state of feeling.

name: Karl Ove Knausgård
teaser: The Norwegian writer whose six-volume My Struggle became a literary event — a memoir-novel of radical honesty that turns washing dishes and remembering a father into gripping, ordinary revelation.

exploreAction.targetName: My Struggle, Book One, opening
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of My Struggle. Notice how Knausgård's attention to the mundane becomes hypnotic. Write what total candor costs and gives a writer — and why the smallest details can carry the largest grief.

name: Henning Mankell
teaser: The Swedish crime writer who made the police procedural literary. His Kurt Wallander novels map the underside of Swedish welfare society — melancholy, migration, and a detective who feels the cold of the world.

exploreAction.targetName: Faceless Killers, opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Faceless Killers. Notice how the crime arrives inside a landscape of isolation — snow, dawn, an empty farmhouse. Write how Mankell uses the mystery to ask what a society hides from itself.

name: Stieg Larsson
teaser: The Swedish journalist whose Millennium trilogy — The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and its sequels — became a global phenomenon. Lisbeth Salander is modern crime fiction's most iconic outsider.

exploreAction.targetName: The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo, prologue
exploreAction.instruction: Read the prologue, set in the 1960s. Notice how Larsson builds a cold, corporate world where power hides abuse. Write how the novel's twin heroes — journalist and hacker — approach the same corruption from opposite sides.

name: Fredrik Backman
teaser: The Swedish author of A Man Called Ove and Anxious People — warm, funny novels about grumpy people and the communities that insist on loving them. Best-sellers that smuggle in real grief.

exploreAction.targetName: A Man Called Ove, opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of A Man Called Ove. Notice how Backman makes a rigid, complaining man immediately endearing. Write how comedy and tenderness share the same sentences, and what the novel says about grief and routine.

name: Pär Lagerkvist
teaser: The Swedish Nobel laureate who asked the big questions in small, stark books. Barabbas retells the crucifixion from the released murderer's bewildered point of view — faith as absence, doubt as presence.

exploreAction.targetName: Barabbas, opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Barabbas. Notice how Lagerkvist keeps the style bare and biblical. Write what it means to be the man who lived instead of Christ — how does the novel make doubt itself a form of searching?

name: Astrid Lindgren
teaser: The Swedish children's author who redefined childhood on the page — Pippi Longstocking, the Children of Noisy Village, and the fierce brothers of the Lionheart. She trusted children with grief and freedom.

exploreAction.targetName: Pippi Longstocking, first chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Pippi Longstocking. Notice how Pippi breaks every rule of the polite village without malice. Write how Lindgren's anarchic heroine made room for children's power, imagination, and kindness on their own terms.

name: Tove Jansson
teaser: The Finnish-Swedish artist who created the Moomins — and wrote adult fiction of equal subtlety. Her Moominvalley books are philosophical comfort objects, and her later stories are sharp, quiet masterpieces.

exploreAction.targetName: The Summer Book, a chapter
exploreAction.instruction: Read a chapter of The Summer Book, about a grandmother and granddaughter on a Finnish island. Notice how Jansson renders the natural world with precise, unshowy detail. Write what the island teaches about attention and letting go.

name: Mika Waltari
teaser: The Finnish novelist of The Egyptian — one of the best-selling historical novels ever, a court physician's confession set in the Egypt of the pharaohs, full of immortality, plague, and human weakness.

exploreAction.targetName: The Egyptian, opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of The Egyptian. Notice how Waltari frames the tale as a memoir written by a man who has lost everything. Write how the ancient setting lets him discuss timeless questions of ambition, love, and death.

name: Arto Paasilinna
teaser: The Finnish novelist of deadpan absurdity. The Year of the Hare follows a journalist who chucks it all to chase a hare across Finland — a comic ode to escape, wilderness, and saying no to everything.

exploreAction.targetName: The Year of the Hare, opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of The Year of the Hare. Notice how Paasilinna keeps a straight face through increasingly surreal events. Write how the hare functions as a living excuse for freedom, and what the novel says about modern life.

name: Halldór Laxness
teaser: The Icelandic Nobel laureate who wrote Independent People — the story of Bjartur of Summerhouses, a sheep farmer who would rather starve than owe anyone, in one of the greatest novels about stubbornness.

exploreAction.targetName: Independent People, opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Independent People. Notice how Laxness treats Bjartur's epic pride with both comedy and awe. Write what 'independence' costs the man who insists on it — and what it buys him.

name: Jón Kalman Stefánsson
teaser: The Icelandic novelist of sea, snow, and story — Summer Light, and Then Comes the Night and his trilogy about a boy who carries a book into the cold. His prose is both brutal and tender.

exploreAction.targetName: Summer Light, and Then Comes the Night, opening
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of the novel, which begins with a village and its restless residents. Notice how Stefánsson moves between voices and moods like weather. Write how the small town becomes a whole cosmos of longing.

name: Peter Høeg
teaser: The Danish novelist of Smilla's Sense of Snow — an arctic thriller about a woman who knows snow the way others know faces, and uses that knowledge to solve a murder the authorities would rather bury.

exploreAction.targetName: Smilla's Sense of Snow, opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Smilla's Sense of Snow. Notice how Smilla's expertise — snow, ice, footprints — becomes the engine of the plot. Write how a special form of attention becomes both identity and method of truth.

name: Sigrid Combüchen
teaser: The Swedish-German novelist and essayist whose books — like The White Lie and About Beauty — are intricate, witty examinations of art, biography, and how stories get told and mistold.

exploreAction.targetName: The White Lie, opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of The White Lie. Notice how Combüchen frames her narrator's unreliable memory as the subject itself. Write how the novel questions what we allow ourselves to believe about our own lives and art.

name: Lars Saabye Christensen
teaser: The Norwegian novelist of The Half Brother — a sprawling, funny, painful family saga set in Oslo after the war. His Beatles follows four boys growing up with the band and a changing Norway.

exploreAction.targetName: Beatles, opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Beatles. Notice how Christensen catches the texture of a 1960s Oslo childhood — music, nicknames, small rebellions. Write how a pop band becomes the soundtrack and measure of growing up.

name: Jonas Lie
teaser: One of the four great figures of 19th-century Norwegian literature, alongside Ibsen, Bjørnson, and Kielland. His novels of seafaring families, like The Pilot and His Wife, made the coastal world feel mythic.

exploreAction.targetName: The Pilot and His Wife, opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of The Pilot and His Wife. Notice how Lie makes the sea, the fjord, and the ship feel like extensions of his characters' inner lives. Write how the coastal setting shapes ambition and love in the novel.

name: Jens Peter Jacobsen
teaser: The Danish novelist and poet whose Niels Lyhne was a Bible for the European fin-de-siècle — a portrait of an atheist, a dreamer, and a failure that Rilke and others could not stop reading.

exploreAction.targetName: Niels Lyhne, opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Niels Lyhne. Notice how Jacobsen's prose is lyrical and precise at once, and how his hero drifts between aspiration and passivity. Write how the novel made 'a life without illusions' feel both noble and sad.

name: Vilhelm Moberg
teaser: The Swedish novelist of The Emigrants series — the four-volume epic of a family leaving Småland for America in the 1850s. A people's history of emigration, written with immense warmth and plain grandeur.

exploreAction.targetName: The Emigrants, opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of The Emigrants. Notice how Moberg grounds the decision to leave in the soil, the harvest, and the potato patch. Write how the novel makes you feel both the weight of home and the terror of departure.

name: Inger Edelfeldt
teaser: The Swedish novelist and translator, a boundary-crossing figure of Nordic letters whose fiction and essays have probed identity, migration, and the art of living between cultures and languages.

exploreAction.targetName: Inger Edelfeldt, a short story or essay
exploreAction.instruction: Read one of Edelfeldt's shorter works. Notice how identity is never settled in her fiction. Write how living between languages or cultures shapes a writer's sense of self, and how her work makes that visible.

name: Lu Xun
teaser: The founding father of modern Chinese literature. His story Diary of a Madman and his essay on the 'iron house' diagnosed China's sickness with savage wit. Every Chinese writer since has had to answer him.

exploreAction.targetName: Diary of a Madman, the full story
exploreAction.instruction: Read Diary of a Madman. Notice how the narrator's paranoia gradually becomes the reader's clarity about a society that eats people metaphorically and literally. Write how the 'madman' is the sanest person in the story.

name: Mo Yan
teaser: The Chinese Nobel laureate whose novels — Red Sorghum, Life and Death Are Wearing Me Out — are sprawling, sensual, magical chronicles of rural China. His narrator famously declared, 'I have a true story to tell.'.

exploreAction.targetName: Red Sorghum, opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Red Sorghum. Notice how Mo Yan immerses the reader in the smell and heat of the sorghum fields and the violence of the war years. Write how sensory excess carries history and legend at once.

name: Yu Hua
teaser: The Chinese novelist of To Live — the devastating saga of a man who survives every loss history can throw at him. Also wrote the darkly comic Brothers. His prose is plain, brutal, and deeply tender.

exploreAction.targetName: To Live, opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of To Live. Notice how Fugui's fortunes fall with a gambler's inevitability. Write how Yu Hua makes one man's losses into a record of a century, and what 'to live' means in the book's final accounting.

name: Cao Xueqin
teaser: The 18th-century author of Dream of the Red Chamber, the great novel of Chinese literature — a family's grandeur and ruin, told through a boy's love, a girl's poetry, and the fall of a clan.

exploreAction.targetName: Dream of the Red Chamber, the opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of the novel, with its frame of stone and dream and the household of the Jia family. Notice how the mundane and the mythic interweave. Write why this book is called the Chinese 'great novel' and what it mourns.

name: Eileen Chang
teaser: The Chinese writer of 1940s Shanghai whose stories of love, betrayal, and survival are among the sharpest ever written about urban life. Love in a Fallen City and Lust, Caution earned her a devoted afterlife.

exploreAction.targetName: Love in a Fallen City, opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Love in a Fallen City. Notice how Chang's prose is diamond-hard and wry, and how her lovers negotiate like businessmen. Write how the fall of Hong Kong becomes the story's strange happy ending.

name: Kenzaburō Ōe
teaser: The Japanese Nobel laureate who turned his family and his nation's trauma into fiction — A Personal Matter about a father of a disabled son, and The Silent Cry about a village's revolt. Fierce, guilt-ridden, humane.

exploreAction.targetName: A Personal Matter, opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of A Personal Matter. Notice how Ōe's protagonist tries to escape his new responsibility through a fantasy of flight. Write how the novel makes a private crisis inseparable from public history — Hiroshima, guilt, survival.

name: Ryūnosuke Akutagawa
teaser: The Japanese master of the short story — Rashomon and In a Grove (the basis of Kurosawa's film) probe truth, selfishness, and the masks people wear. He killed himself at 35, haunted by madness.

exploreAction.targetName: Rashomon and In a Grove
exploreAction.instruction: Read both stories. Notice how Akutagawa withholds a single truth and offers competing testimonies instead. Write how In a Grove questions whether any account — including our own — is ever simply true.

name: Osamu Dazai
teaser: The Japanese novelist of No Longer Human — a confessional masterpiece of alienation that became a bible for disaffected readers. Dazai's life of drinking and affairs shadowed his work, which keeps its terrible lucidity.

exploreAction.targetName: No Longer Human, opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of No Longer Human, where the narrator recalls being a child who performed happiness. Notice how Dazai's confessions feel both sincere and staged. Write how the book's title names a specific kind of exile.

name: Natsume Sōseki
teaser: The giant of modern Japanese literature — I Am a Cat, Kokoro, and Botchan balance comedy and loneliness. He watched Japan modernize and worried about what the West was doing to its soul.

exploreAction.targetName: Kokoro, the opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Kokoro. Notice how the narrator's relationship with Sensei is built from reticence and hints. Write how Sōseki's novel of a secret guilt explores the gap between the modern and the traditional self.

name: Shūsaku Endō
teaser: The Japanese Catholic novelist of Silence — a priest in 17th-century Japan who must choose between apostasy and martyrdom. Endō's questions about faith, weakness, and the face of God made him a world writer.

exploreAction.targetName: Silence, the opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Silence. Notice how Endō builds the story from letters and travel into a landscape of fear. Write what the novel suggests about a God who seems silent in suffering, and whether weakness can be a form of faithfulness.

name: Keigo Higashino
teaser: The Japanese master of the puzzle mystery — The Devotion of Suspect X and Malice are emotional, ingeniously plotted novels that have sold in the millions. He turned the whodunit into the why-dunit.

exploreAction.targetName: The Devotion of Suspect X, opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of The Devotion of Suspect X. Notice how the 'trick' is hidden in full view from the first chapter. Write how Higashino makes the reader care about the criminal's logic as much as the detective's.

name: Miyazawa Kenji
teaser: The Japanese poet and children's author of Night on the Galactic Railroad — a Buddhist, a farmer, and a visionary who saw the cosmos in a field of potatoes. His tales are strange, tender, and vast.

exploreAction.targetName: Night on the Galactic Railroad, opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Night on the Galactic Railroad. Notice how the train journey blends astronomy, grief, and Buddhist ideas of sacrifice. Write what the journey's mysterious ending suggests about life, death, and true happiness.

name: Hwang Sok-yong
teaser: The South Korean novelist of The Guest and Familiar Things — a dissident who lived through dictatorship and prison, and whose fiction braids Korea's modern traumas with folk wisdom and fierce compassion.

exploreAction.targetName: The Guest, opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of The Guest. Notice how Hwang's narrator returns to a divided Korea, carrying both memory and exorcism. Write how the novel treats war and ideology as kinds of possession that must be spoken out.

name: Cho Nam-joo
teaser: The South Korean novelist of Kim Jiyoung, Born 1982 — the quiet, devastating account of one ordinary woman's life that ignited a nationwide reckoning with everyday sexism and became a global phenomenon.

exploreAction.targetName: Kim Jiyoung, Born 1982, opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Kim Jiyoung, Born 1982. Notice how Cho narrates a life in neutral clinical prose, and how that tone itself becomes the indictment. Write how documenting the ordinary can expose systemic harm.

name: Ko Un
teaser: The South Korean poet who lived through war, the dictatorship years, and prison — and produced tens of thousands of poems, from the epic Ten Thousand Lives to searing political verse and Zen-flavored stillness.

exploreAction.targetName: Ko Un's poems, a small selection
exploreAction.instruction: Read a handful of Ko Un's short poems. Notice how the smallest image — a weed, a stone, a monk's bowl — carries enormous weight. Write how poetry can hold both political anger and quiet Buddhist attention at once.

name: Yi Mun-yol
teaser: The South Korean novelist of Our Twisted Hero and The Poet — books that dissect power, corruption, and the moral compromises of modern Korean history with chilly, elegant prose.

exploreAction.targetName: Our Twisted Hero, the full novella
exploreAction.instruction: Read Our Twisted Hero. Notice how the classroom tyranny of the student boss mirrors larger systems of power. Write how Yi makes a schoolroom a parable of dictatorship — and how the twist complicates simple judgments.

name: Munshi Premchand
teaser: The giant of Hindi and Urdu fiction — Godan (The Gift of a Cow) follows a peasant's impossible struggle for a cow and dignity. He wrote the stories of India's poor with unsentimental compassion.

exploreAction.targetName: Godan, opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Godan. Notice how Premchand renders village economics — debt, caste, weather — with exactness. Write how Hori's longing for a cow becomes a measure of dignity, and what the novel says about debt's grip.

name: Saadat Hasan Manto
teaser: The Urdu writer of Partition who refused to look away — Toba Tek Singh and Cold Meat are explosive stories about madness, borders, and the body. He was tried for obscenity six times; he never stopped writing.

exploreAction.targetName: Toba Tek Singh, the full story
exploreAction.instruction: Read Toba Tek Singh, set in an asylum being divided between India and Pakistan. Notice how the inmates' confusion mirrors the nations' logic. Write how Manto uses absurdity to indict the border itself — and who 'the sane' really are.

name: Cao Yu
teaser: China's greatest modern playwright — Thunderstorm, a family tragedy of secrets and class set in a suffocating mansion, is a landmark of Chinese theatre and still staged constantly.

exploreAction.targetName: Thunderstorm, Act One
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first act of Thunderstorm. Notice how Cao Yu sets the weather, the servants, and the hidden family ties in motion before the storm breaks. Write how the play uses class and secrecy to build toward catastrophe.

name: Hwang Jini
teaser: The legendary 16th-century Korean poet and gisaeng whose sijo verses are among the most loved in the language — poems of love, wit, and freedom composed at the edge of a strict Confucian world.

exploreAction.targetName: Hwang Jini's sijo poems
exploreAction.instruction: Read a selection of Hwang Jini's sijo. Notice how each three-line verse turns on a clever pivot — often at the reader's expense. Write what her poems reveal about wit as a form of freedom for a woman of her time.

name: Li Bai
teaser: China's most beloved poet — the Tang dynasty's drunken, wandering, moon-loving immortal. His poems of friendship, wine, and exile are memorized by every Chinese schoolchild and live on in the world's imagination.

exploreAction.targetName: Li Bai's poems, a small selection
exploreAction.instruction: Read a handful of Li Bai's poems, including Drinking Alone by Moonlight. Notice how his lines move with effortless lightness. Write what the poems' freedom and loneliness suggest about the figure of the wanderer-poet.

name: Du Fu
teaser: Li Bai's great friend and China's poet of history — Du Fu wrote through war, exile, and hunger, and his poetry became the conscience of the nation. His careful craftsmanship frames an enormous empathy.

exploreAction.targetName: Du Fu's poems, a small selection
exploreAction.instruction: Read three of Du Fu's poems, including one from the war years. Notice how precise observation and pity share the same line. Write how Du Fu's poetry differs from Li Bai's — where one flies, the other stays to record.

name: Choi Seung-ja
teaser: A pioneering South Korean poet whose frank, image-rich verse broke the decorum of Korean poetry in the 1980s — writing about the body, desire, and daily life with startling directness.

exploreAction.targetName: Choi Seung-ja's poems, a selection
exploreAction.instruction: Read a few of Choi Seung-ja's poems. Notice how the domestic and the bodily enter the poem without apology. Write what her directness meant for a generation of Korean women readers and writers.

name: Juan Rulfo
teaser: The Mexican writer who published almost nothing — but Pedro Páramo and The Burning Plain changed world literature. A village where the dead speak, and prose as dry and haunted as the dust.

exploreAction.targetName: Pedro Páramo, the opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Pedro Páramo. Notice how the dead narrator and the living traveler blur, and how the village of Comala is described as heat and murmur. Write how Rulfo builds a landscape where the afterlife is just another room.

name: José Saramago
teaser: The Portuguese Nobel laureate who wrote without conventional punctuation — long rivers of speech that pull you under. Blindness and Baltasar and Blimunda explore civilization's skin-thin veneer with rage and tenderness.

exploreAction.targetName: Blindness, the opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Blindness. Notice how the white blindness spreads from one man to a city, and how Saramago's run-on prose mirrors contagion. Write what the novel says about the social contract when everyone loses sight.

name: Fernando Pessoa
teaser: The Portuguese poet who wrote as many selves — heteronyms with their own biographies and styles: the modernist Álvaro de Campos, the neoclassical Ricardo Reis, the humble Alberto Caeiro. The Book of Disquiet is his strange masterpiece.

exploreAction.targetName: The Book of Disquiet, a selection
exploreAction.instruction: Read a selection of fragments from The Book of Disquiet. Notice how Pessoa's assistant bookkeeper narrator dreams instead of acts. Write how writing as invented selves might be a way to live many lives — or none at all.

name: Jorge Amado
teaser: The Brazilian novelist of Bahia — Dona Flor and Her Two Husbands, Gabriela, Clove and Cinnamon. He filled his pages with heat, humor, food, and the street wisdom of the poor. His books sold in the millions.

exploreAction.targetName: Gabriela, Clove and Cinnamon, opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Gabriela, Clove and Cinnamon. Notice how Amado makes the town of Ilhéus — its cacao, its customs, its gossip — the real main character. Write how food, scent, and weather carry the novel's sensuality.

name: Pablo Neruda
teaser: The Chilean Nobel laureate — poet of love sonnets, odes to onions and socks, and the epic Canto General about Latin America's earth and history. He made poetry democratic, sensual, and political.

exploreAction.targetName: Twenty Love Poems, a selection, and an Ode
exploreAction.instruction: Read a few love poems and one ode (try Ode to the Onion or Ode to My Socks). Notice how Neruda makes the humble object magnificent. Write how the odes find the sacred in the everyday, and why that is a political act too.

name: Octavio Paz
teaser: The Mexican Nobel laureate — poet and essayist whose The Labyrinth of Solitude dissected Mexican identity, and whose poems (Sunstone, Blanco) are among the century's most beautiful meditations on time and love.

exploreAction.targetName: Sunstone, the long poem
exploreAction.instruction: Read Sunstone. Notice how the poem's circular form loops the same line back after 584 verses. Write how Paz's meditation on a single moment — a woman, a room, the Aztec calendar — expands into all of history.

name: Horacio Quiroga
teaser: The Uruguayan master of the jungle story — his Tales of Love, Madness and Death and Jungle Tales turn the Misiones wilderness into a place of terrifying beauty. His life was as violent as his fiction.

exploreAction.targetName: The Decapitated Chicken, and one jungle tale
exploreAction.instruction: Read The Decapitated Chicken. Notice how Quiroga builds horror out of domestic detail and heredity. Write how his stories use the natural world as both refuge and threat, and what the title story says about obsession.

name: Adolfo Bioy Casares
teaser: The Argentine novelist and Borges's closest collaborator — The Invention of Morel is a perfect little novel about love, islands, and a machine that replays the past. Borges called it flawless.

exploreAction.targetName: The Invention of Morel, opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of The Invention of Morel. Notice how the castaway narrator's observations slowly decode the island's ghostly visitors. Write how the novel turns science fiction into a meditation on love and mortality.

name: José Donoso
teaser: The Chilean novelist of The Obscene Bird of Night — a labyrinthine, Gothic masterwork about an old woman, her monsters, and the house where servants mimic their masters. Latin America's strangest novel of power.

exploreAction.targetName: The Obscene Bird of Night, opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of The Obscene Bird of Night. Notice how identity dissolves and multiplies, and how the house breathes. Write how Donoso uses the grotesque to explore the master-servant relationship at the heart of his society.

name: Silvina Ocampo
teaser: The Argentine short-story writer and poet — Borges and Bioy's collaborator, whose stories twist childhood, cruelty, and the fantastic into glittering, disturbing miniatures. Rediscovered as a hidden giant.

exploreAction.targetName: Silvina Ocampo, a handful of stories
exploreAction.instruction: Read two or three of Ocampo's short stories. Notice how her child narrators observe adult cruelty with unsettling calm. Write what her fiction suggests about innocence — is it ever really innocent, or just another mask?

name: Alejandra Pizarnik
teaser: The Argentine poet of darkness and desire — her short, intense poems face the night, the mirror, and silence without blinking. She died at 36, and her voice has only grown louder.

exploreAction.targetName: Pizarnik's poems, a small selection
exploreAction.instruction: Read a handful of Pizarnik's poems. Notice how few words she needs to create a whole night. Write what her poetry says about the desire to be seen and the fear of being seen, and why that tension still resonates.

name: Federico García Lorca
teaser: The Andalusian poet and playwright — Blood Wedding, Yerma, and The House of Bernarda Alba turned Spanish rural tragedy into timeless theatre. He was murdered by Franco's men in 1936 at 38.

exploreAction.targetName: Blood Wedding, Act One
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first act of Blood Wedding. Notice how the knife, the moon, and the lullaby carry the coming violence. Write how Lorca blends folk poetry and tragedy, and what the play says about desire against the law of the family.

name: Javier Marías
teaser: The Spanish novelist of A Heart So White and All Souls — a master of the long, digressive, hypnotic sentence and of stories told through what people almost said. Also a sharp essayist and translator.

exploreAction.targetName: A Heart So White, opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of A Heart So White, which begins with a woman's suicide during her honeymoon. Notice how Marías circles events without ever quite landing on them. Write how the withheld telling becomes its own kind of suspense.

name: Carmen Laforet
teaser: The Spanish novelist who, at 23, wrote Nada — a devastating portrait of postwar Barcelona and a girl's arrival into a house full of ghosts. It won the first Nadal Prize and changed Spanish fiction.

exploreAction.targetName: Nada, the opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Nada. Notice how Andrea arrives in the dark city and the claustrophobic apartment. Write how Laforet makes hunger, poverty, and a family's decay feel like weather pressing on one girl.

name: Arturo Pérez-Reverte
teaser: The Spanish novelist of The Club Dumas and the Captain Alatriste series — swashbuckling, erudite, and dark. A former war correspondent, he writes about honor, books, and the sea with equal passion.

exploreAction.targetName: The Club Dumas, opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of The Club Dumas. Notice how Pérez-Reverte treats rare books as objects of obsession and danger. Write how the novel blends detective story, book history, and the occult into a single page-turning engine.

name: Carlos Ruiz Zafón
teaser: The Spanish author of The Shadow of the Wind — a love letter to Barcelona and to books, set in a Cemetery of Forgotten Books. It became one of the best-selling Spanish novels ever written.

exploreAction.targetName: The Shadow of the Wind, opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of The Shadow of the Wind. Notice how the Cemetery of Forgotten Books is described as a holy place for readers. Write how the novel makes the act of choosing a book — and losing one — into a mystery.

name: Rosa Montero
teaser: The Spanish novelist and journalist whose fiction — The Lunatic of the House, Weep, My Lady — braids journalism, fantasy, and autobiography into a search for how stories keep us alive.

exploreAction.targetName: The Lunatic of the House, opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of The Lunatic of the House. Notice how Montero's narrator invents an alter ego to explore her own fears and desires. Write how the novel uses fantasy as a tool for honesty rather than escape.

name: Rosa Chacel
teaser: The Spanish novelist in the line of the great modernists — her dense, introspective fiction, like The Maravillas District, explores memory and the female self. She spent decades of exile in Brazil.

exploreAction.targetName: The Maravillas District, opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of The Maravillas District. Notice how Chacel's prose moves by association, circling memory rather than narrating it. Write how her experimental style gives access to an inner life that traditional realism flattens.

name: Rosario Castellanos
teaser: The Mexican writer and diplomat who wrote about women and indigenous life with irony and fury — The Book of Lamentations and her poems are essential reading for understanding Mexico's inner fractures.

exploreAction.targetName: The Book of Lamentations, opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of The Book of Lamentations. Notice how Castellanos gives voice to a Tzotzil woman's rebellion against both church and state. Write how the novel weaves colonial history into one woman's fierce refusal.

name: Elena Poniatowska
teaser: The Polish-born Mexican journalist and novelist of The Night of Tlatelolco — the oral history of the 1968 massacre that made her Mexico's conscience. Also wrote the dazzling biography Dear Diego.

exploreAction.targetName: The Night of Tlatelolco, opening sections
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of The Night of Tlatelolco. Notice how Poniatowska stitches together testimonies, slogans, and official lies. Write how oral history as a literary form can do what official accounts refuse to.

name: Rosa Regàs
teaser: The Spanish novelist and publisher — a free spirit of the Barcelona literary scene whose novels like Azul explore passion, memory, and the life of a woman who refuses the roles handed to her.

exploreAction.targetName: Azul, opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Azul. Notice how Regàs weaves present and past, and how the sea functions as both setting and memory. Write how the novel uses recollection to measure what a woman's freedom has cost her.

name: Aeschylus
teaser: The father of Greek tragedy — he added a second actor to what was a one-man chorus, inventing drama as dialogue. His Oresteia is the only surviving trilogy from the ancient stage, and it takes revenge, law and mercy from myth into politics. He fought at Marathon and asked that his gravestone mention only that.

exploreAction.targetName: The Oresteia — the trilogy that invents justice
exploreAction.instruction: Read Agamemnon first and notice how the chorus slows everything down — that's the oldest layer of drama, the single voice that tragedy grew out of. Then watch how Aeschylus hands the story to actors and never looks back.

name: Sophocles
teaser: The middle of the three great tragedians, the one who perfected the form — he added the third actor and wrote Oedipus Rex, the play Aristotle called the perfect tragedy. He won the Dionysia festival more than any other playwright, at least 24 times. He also served as a general and a priest, and lived to 90 in a city that barely made old bones.

exploreAction.targetName: Oedipus Rex — the tragedy that defines tragedy
exploreAction.instruction: Read Oedipus knowing the ending — the power is not the surprise but the structure, every clue a nail in the trap. Aristotle used this play to define what tragedy is, and nobody has improved the definition.

name: Euripides
teaser: The iconoclast of Greek tragedy — he put women, slaves and doubt on the stage, and Athens booed him for it. His Medea kills her children onstage; his Trojan Women is a war-crime indictment; his Bacchae is a horror movie. He won the festival only five times, died in Macedonia, and after his death his plays outdrew everyone's.

exploreAction.targetName: Medea — the tragedy of the woman who refuses to be a victim
exploreAction.instruction: Read Medea and notice how Euripides makes the monster the most sympathetic voice in the room. That's his whole project: taking the myth and asking what the villain was feeling.

name: Aristophanes
teaser: The great comic playwright of Athens — crude, brilliant, and surgically political. Lysistrata has the women of Greece withhold sex to end the Peloponnesian War; The Clouds savages Socrates; The Frogs brings Aeschylus and Euripides back from the dead to duel. His comedies are the only complete picture we have of how ordinary Athenians talked and joked.

exploreAction.targetName: Lysistrata — the sex strike that ends a war
exploreAction.instruction: Read Lysistrata for the jokes, then for the politics — the profanity is the point. Aristophanes could get away with mocking the city's leaders onstage because comedy was Athens's civic safety valve.

name: Sappho
teaser: The tenth Muse, as Plato called her — a poet of Lesbos whose lyrics about love are so intense that the word 'sapphic' derives from her. Only fragments survive: one complete poem out of nine books, yet those shards are among the most loved lines in all of literature. She ran a circle of young women for whom she wrote marriage songs and love poems. The ancients ranked her with Homer.

exploreAction.targetName: The fragments of Sappho — the most famous broken poems in the world
exploreAction.instruction: Read the fragments aloud — the sounds carry the feeling even where the sense breaks off. Sappho's 'He seems to me equal to the gods' is a whole philosophy of jealousy in seven lines.

name: Virgil
teaser: Rome's national poet — he spent eleven years on the Aeneid, the epic that gave Rome a past, a destiny and Aeneas, the founder-hero who carries his father on his back. He asked for the poem to be burned when he died; Augustus overruled him. Dante made Virgil his guide through hell, which is the highest compliment literature has ever paid.

exploreAction.targetName: The Aeneid — Rome's founding epic
exploreAction.instruction: Read Book II first — the fall of Troy — where Virgil's sympathy for the losers undermines his epic of winners. That tension is why the poem still lives.

name: Ovid
teaser: The poet of transformation — his Metamorphoses is a compendium of every myth in which someone becomes something else: a girl becomes a laurel, a boy becomes a flower, a weaver becomes a spider. Exiled by Augustus to the Black Sea for reasons he never dared state, he spent his last years writing poems of complaint. Shakespeare read him; everyone read him.

exploreAction.targetName: Metamorphoses — the book of changes
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening cosmogony then jump to any myth you know — Daphne, Narcissus, Pygmalion. Ovid's storytelling is the source for half of Western art's plots.

name: Horace
teaser: The poet of moderation — 'golden mean', 'seize the day', 'poetry is sweet and useful': his phrases are Latin proverbs we still quote. The son of a freedman, he rose to be the friend of Augustus and the emperor's poet, yet his best poems are about small pleasures: a farm, a friend, a jar of wine. His Odes are the most polished verse in Latin.

exploreAction.targetName: The Odes of Horace — the poetry of the golden mean
exploreAction.instruction: Read the 'Carpe diem' ode (1.11) then the Soracte ode (1.9) — winter, fire, and the shortness of life. Horace's advice is 2000 years old and still the best available.

name: Catullus
teaser: The first Roman poet of private feeling — he wrote about his affair with 'Lesbia' (a real married woman) in poems that swing from ecstasy to contempt, sometimes in the same line. His poem 5, 'Let us live, my Lesbia, and love', is the most famous love poem in Latin. He also wrote the rudest verse in the classical canon. He died at 30.

exploreAction.targetName: The poems of Catullus — Rome's first love letters
exploreAction.instruction: Read poem 5 aloud, then poem 101, written at his brother's grave — the tenderness next to the profanity is the whole Catullus.

name: Geoffrey Chaucer
teaser: The father of English poetry — he wrote The Canterbury Tales when English was still a peasant language and Latin and French were the tongues of literature. His pilgrims — the Wife of Bath, the Miller, the Pardoner — are the first real characters in English fiction. He was a courtier, diplomat and customs official; the Tales were his side project that outlived the court.

exploreAction.targetName: The Canterbury Tales — England's first great book
exploreAction.instruction: Start with the General Prologue and meet the pilgrims — Chaucer gives each one a face, a flaw and a story. Then read the Wife of Bath's tale, the most modern thing written before 1700.

name: John Milton
teaser: The blind poet who wrote Paradise Lost — the last great epic in the European tradition, dictated to his daughters after he went blind at 44. His Satan is the most seductive villain in literature, and his God the hardest to like; readers have argued about which side Milton was on for 350 years. He also wrote the pamphlet that argued for freedom of the press, Areopagitica.

exploreAction.targetName: Paradise Lost — the epic of the fallen angel
exploreAction.instruction: Read Book I and meet Satan on the burning lake — the speech 'Better to reign in Hell than serve in Heaven' is the most famous defiance in literature. Then decide whether Milton admires him.

name: John Donne
teaser: The metaphysical poet — he wrote love poems that argue like sermons and sermons that burn like love poems. 'No man is an island', 'for whom the bell tolls', 'death, thou shalt die': his lines are the English language's most quoted. He was a brilliant young rake who became an Anglican priest and the most famous preacher of his age. His Holy Sonnets are addressed to God with terrifying intimacy.

exploreAction.targetName: The Holy Sonnets and love poems of John Donne
exploreAction.instruction: Read 'The Flea' for the wit, then 'Death be not proud' for the defiance — Donne never writes one feeling when he can stack three arguments and a pun on top of it.

name: Alexander Pope
teaser: The poet of the Augustan age — tiny, sickly, Catholic in Protestant England, and the sharpest wit of his century. His Essay on Criticism gave us 'fools rush in where angels fear to tread'; his Dunciad is a masterpiece of literary revenge; his translation of Homer paid for a villa. He wrote in heroic couplets that click like a clock.

exploreAction.targetName: The Rape of the Lock — the mock-epic of a stolen curl
exploreAction.instruction: Read The Rape of the Lock, where a hair theft becomes a war of gods and sylphs — Pope invented the mock-epic to make a social slight eternal.

name: William Wordsworth
teaser: The poet who made nature a religion — his Lyrical Ballads with Coleridge in 1798 is usually dated as the start of English Romanticism. He walked the Lake District for decades and wrote about daffodils, leeches and the growth of a poet's mind. He said poetry is 'emotion recollected in tranquillity'. He became poet laureate and grew conservative, which his admirers never forgave.

exploreAction.targetName: Lyrical Ballads — the book that started Romanticism
exploreAction.instruction: Read 'Tintern Abbey' slowly — it is the poem where Wordsworth explains what nature did to him, and what he fears losing. Then 'I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud', which everyone knows and no one has read properly.

name: Samuel Taylor Coleridge
teaser: The poet of the supernatural — Kubla Khan came to him in an opium dream and broke off mid-line when a visitor interrupted; The Rime of the Ancient Mariner is the greatest ballad in English. With Wordsworth he wrote Lyrical Ballads. His opium addiction and his failed marriage shadowed a mind that might have been the most original of the age. His criticism invented close reading.

exploreAction.targetName: The Rime of the Ancient Mariner — the ballad of guilt and the albatross
exploreAction.instruction: Read the Mariner aloud for the music — 'water, water, every where' — then read the marginal gloss Coleridge added, a second voice arguing with the poem.

name: Lord Byron
teaser: The first celebrity poet — 'mad, bad, and dangerous to know', as his lover put it. He swam the Hellespont, fought for Greek independence, had a scandalous affair with his half-sister, and died of fever in Greece at 36. His Childe Harold made the brooding 'Byronic hero' the template for every romantic antihero since. His Don Juan is a comic epic that mocks everything, including himself.

exploreAction.targetName: Childe Harold's Pilgrimage — the poem that made Byron a celebrity
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first canto and meet the weary wanderer — Byron's invention of himself. Then read Don Juan's first canto, where the hero of feeling turns out to be a joke.

name: Percy Bysshe Shelley
teaser: The most radical of the Romantics — atheist, vegetarian, republican, expelled from Oxford for a pamphlet against religion. His Ozymandias mocks empire in fourteen lines; his Prometheus Unbound rewrites the Greek myth as revolution. He drowned at 29 in a storm off Italy. His heart was snatched from the funeral pyre and kept by his wife Mary; it is buried in a different grave from his body.

exploreAction.targetName: Ozymandias and the odes of Shelley
exploreAction.instruction: Read Ozymandias three times — it is the most efficient demolition of tyrants ever written. Then 'To a Skylark' to hear the poet of radical hope.

name: John Keats
teaser: The poet who died at 25 and became the symbol of beauty's brevity — 'a thing of beauty is a joy forever'. A doctor's apprentice who chose poetry, he wrote his greatest odes in one astonishing year, then died of tuberculosis in Rome, asking that his grave read only 'Here lies one whose name was writ in water'. His letters are the most beloved in English.

exploreAction.targetName: The odes of Keats — to autumn, to a nightingale, to a Grecian urn
exploreAction.instruction: Read 'Ode on a Grecian Urn' and stop at the last two lines — 'Beauty is truth, truth beauty' — then decide whether the poem believes itself. Keats called this his 'negative capability', the art of being in doubt.

name: Alfred Lord Tennyson
teaser: The voice of the Victorian age — poet laureate for 42 years, the longest ever. In Memoriam mourns his best friend with such precision that it became the age's book of grief; The Charge of the Light Brigade made a military blunder into national honor; Ulysses gives old age its most stirring speech. His poems were memorized in every schoolroom in Britain.

exploreAction.targetName: In Memoriam — the poem that taught Victorians to grieve
exploreAction.instruction: Read Ulysses first — 'to strive, to seek, to find, and not to yield' — then the opening of In Memoriam, where doubt and faith argue stanza by stanza.

name: Robert Browning
teaser: The poet of the dramatic monologue — he invented the form where a speaker reveals himself while talking about something else, and it changed poetry forever. 'My Last Duchess' is a murderer explaining himself; 'Fra Lippo Lippi' is a monk defending art. He eloped with Elizabeth Barrett and lived in Italy, where his poetry got sun. Difficult, brilliant, and deeply loved by those who crack him.

exploreAction.targetName: My Last Duchess and the dramatic monologues of Browning
exploreAction.instruction: Read 'My Last Duchess' twice — the duke tells you he killed his wife while sounding perfectly reasonable. Browning's trick is that the speaker always convicts himself.

name: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
teaser: The most famous woman poet of the Victorian age — an invalid who wrote Sonnets from the Portuguese, a sequence of love poems to the man who eloped with her, Robert Browning. 'How do I love thee? Let me count the ways' is the most quoted love line in English. She out-wrote her husband in fame during their lifetime, and campaigned against slavery and child labor.

exploreAction.targetName: Sonnets from the Portuguese — the love sonnets she hid from her husband
exploreAction.instruction: Read sonnet 43 — 'How do I love thee' — then sonnet 1, where she confesses she is writing them. The sequence is a diary of falling in love against all odds.

name: Matthew Arnold
teaser: The poet of Victorian doubt — 'Dover Beach' is the great poem of faith retreating, the 'melancholy, long, withdrawing roar' of the sea of belief. He was a school inspector by day and a critic by night; his essays defined what culture meant for the age. He wrote little, and that little is the age's conscience: beauty at the edge of the dark.

exploreAction.targetName: Dover Beach — the poem of faith's retreat
exploreAction.instruction: Read 'Dover Beach' at dusk and listen for the withdrawing sea — Arnold wrote the Victorian crisis of faith as a sound. Then read his essay 'Culture and Anarchy', the other half of his mind.

name: Gerard Manley Hopkins
teaser: The Jesuit priest who invented sprung rhythm — a meter so physical it sounds like drums, and so strange that his poems were published only after his death, in 1918. 'The Windhover' praises a kestrel and, secretly, Christ; 'Pied Beauty' glorifies a world of dappled, freckled, folded things. He burned his early poems when he joined the priesthood, then couldn't stop writing.

exploreAction.targetName: The Windhover and the poems of Gerard Manley Hopkins
exploreAction.instruction: Read 'The Windhover' aloud and let the rhythm knock — 'the achieve of, the mastery of the thing'. Hopkins's sprung rhythm is the most physical poetry in English.

name: A.E. Housman
teaser: The classicist who wrote A Shropshire Lad — a book of 63 poems about young men dying, soldiers, lovers and suicide, published in 1896 and still in print. He was a professor of Latin who refused to discuss his own poems, and his verses are simple on the surface and desolate underneath. 'When I was one-and-twenty' is the most quoted of them. He never explained why the lads keep dying.

exploreAction.targetName: A Shropshire Lad — the poems of doomed young men
exploreAction.instruction: Read 'When I was one-and-twenty' and feel the rhyme clicking shut like a trap. Housman's simplicity is a mask; every happy line has a graveyard under it.

name: W.B. Yeats
teaser: Ireland's great poet — he moved from Celtic twilight mysticism to the hard, bone-dry poetry of old age without losing a drop of magic. 'The Second Coming' — 'things fall apart; the centre cannot hold' — became the twentieth century's favorite prophecy. He loved Maud Gonne for a lifetime and made unrequited love into a poetic system. He was a senator, a mystic, and a Nobel laureate.

exploreAction.targetName: The Second Coming and the poems of W.B. Yeats
exploreAction.instruction: Read 'The Second Coming' and notice it was written in 1919, before the century confirmed it. Then read 'Sailing to Byzantium', the old poet's farewell to the sensual world.

name: W.H. Auden
teaser: The poet of the age — he wrote 'Musée des Beaux-Arts', about suffering's indifference, and 'Funeral Blues' ('stop all the clocks'), the poem from Four Weddings and a Funeral. He moved from England to America on the eve of World War II and rewrote his early poems for the rest of his life, as if nothing was ever finished. His 'September 1, 1939' has 'we must love one another or die', which he later disowned.

exploreAction.targetName: Musée des Beaux-Arts and the poems of W.H. Auden
exploreAction.instruction: Read 'Musée des Beaux-Arts' next to Bruegel's Fall of Icarus — Auden wrote the poem about the painting, and the painting is about everything. Then 'Funeral Blues', the saddest party poem ever.

name: Dylan Thomas
teaser: The Welsh poet of intoxication — 'Do not go gentle into that good night' is the most quoted poem about dying, written for his dying father. His Under Milk Wood is a play for voices about a Welsh village; his voice was so famous he became a radio star. He drank himself to death in New York at 39, after his reading tour made him an American legend. His prose-poem A Child's Christmas in Wales is a holiday classic.

exploreAction.targetName: Do Not Go Gentle — and the poems of Dylan Thomas
exploreAction.instruction: Read 'Do Not Go Gentle' aloud — the villanelle's repeated lines are a chant against death. Then read 'Fern Hill', the poem of childhood's green light.

name: Philip Larkin
teaser: The poet of the mundane made permanent — he worked as a librarian in Hull for 30 years and wrote about Sundays, ambulances, and the moment after love. 'This Be The Verse' ('they fuck you up, your mum and dad') is his most famous; 'The Whitsun Weddings' his best. He turned down the laureateship, saying it would be 'a terrible idea'. His poems are funny, bleak, and exactly true.

exploreAction.targetName: The Whitsun Weddings — the poems of ordinary England
exploreAction.instruction: Read 'The Whitsun Weddings' and watch a train journey become a national portrait. Then 'An Arundel Tomb', where 'what will survive of us is love' — note the small print.

name: Seamus Heaney
teaser: The poet of bogs, digging and memory — Northern Ireland's great voice, who won the Nobel for poems that turn farm work, violence and language into each other. 'Digging' is his calling card: pen in hand, his father's spade in the earth. He translated Beowulf into a modern classic and his essays are the best criticism of his generation. He is buried in his home parish of Bellaghy.

exploreAction.targetName: Digging and the poems of Seamus Heaney
exploreAction.instruction: Read 'Digging' first — the poem that announces his whole project. Then 'The Grauballe Man', where a bog body becomes the Troubles, becomes myth.

name: Wilfred Owen
teaser: The war poet who wrote the anti-war poems of World War I — 'Dulce et Decorum Est' describes a gas attack with a horror no one had put on paper. 'Anthem for Doomed Youth' counts the dead. He was killed in action a week before the armistice, at 25; his mother received the telegram on Armistice Day itself. His poetry was published posthumously and changed how war is written about.

exploreAction.targetName: Dulce et Decorum Est — the poem that ended the old way of war poetry
exploreAction.instruction: Read 'Dulce et Decorum Est' and then read the Latin tag at the end — Owen is answering Horace's lie with the truth. Then 'Strange Meeting', his poem from the dead.

name: Siegfried Sassoon
teaser: The war poet who said it in prose and verse — he survived the trenches, won the Military Cross, then threw the medal into a river and wrote a public protest against the war. His poem 'They' strips the glory from dying for England; his Memoirs of George Sherston fictionalize his own story. He outlived the war by half a century and kept writing about the men who didn't.

exploreAction.targetName: The war poems of Siegfried Sassoon
exploreAction.instruction: Read 'The General' — fourteen lines that indict the staff officers who sent men to die — then 'Everyone Sang', his one poem of joy after the armistice.

name: Tobias Smollett
teaser: The picaresque novelist of Georgian Britain — Roderick Random and Humphry Clinker send their heroes through a Britain of inns, ships, gaols and highwaymen, narrated with a sailor's bluntness. He was a ship's surgeon, a Scot in London, and a furious polemicist. Humphry Clinker, his last novel, is a comic masterpiece in letters that sends a family around Britain and ends in happiness.

exploreAction.targetName: Humphry Clinker — the novel of a family tour of Britain
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first letters and meet the family — each correspondent sees the same events differently, which is the whole comic engine. Smollett's Scots accent is the first dialect comedy in the novel.

name: Walter Scott
teaser: The inventor of the historical novel — his Waverley (1814) created the form and made him the most famous novelist in Europe, so popular that his publishers went bankrupt and he spent his last years writing to pay them off. Ivanhoe gave us the romantic Middle Ages; Rob Roy gave Scotland its hero. He almost single-handedly made Scotland a tourist destination. His books outsold everyone but Byron.

exploreAction.targetName: Ivanhoe — the novel that invented the Middle Ages
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening tournament scenes and feel the genre being born — nobody had put history this vividly on the page. Then read Rob Roy for the Scotland behind the romance.

name: George Meredith
teaser: The novelist of psychological comedy — The Egoist (1879) dissects a man so in love with himself that courtship becomes vivisection. He was a poet, novelist and editor who championed Hardy when Hardy was unknown. His prose is dense, his wit is dry, and his 'egoist' Sir Willoughby Patterne is one of the great comic monsters of fiction. Virginia Woolf called him a master of the unsaid.

exploreAction.targetName: The Egoist — the comedy of the perfect gentleman
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening where Meredith introduces his hero as 'a gentleman of such eminent good sense' — the irony is the whole book. Then watch Clara Middleton learn to say no.

name: Robert A. Heinlein
teaser: The dean of science fiction — Starship Troopers, Stranger in a Strange Land and The Moon Is a Harsh Mistress made him the genre's most influential mind. He wrote the first sci-fi novel to hit the bestseller lists seriously, and his ideas — libertarian, contrarian, always arguing — are still being fought over. He also wrote the classic juveniles that recruited a generation into the genre.

exploreAction.targetName: The Moon Is a Harsh Mistress — the novel of revolution on the moon
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first chapter and meet Mike, the computer who wakes up — Heinlein's politics are in every sentence. Then Stranger in a Strange Land, the book that gave the 60s a vocabulary.

name: Dean Koontz
teaser: The thriller writer who has sold over 500 million books — Watchers, Intensity and Odd Thomas mix horror, suspense and a stubborn optimism. He wrote his first novel as a young man and for years was compared to Stephen King; his voice is warmer, his monsters more often human. He has written over 100 books and still produces several a year from his California home.

exploreAction.targetName: Watchers — the thriller about the dog, the monster and the spy
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters and meet Einstein the dog, who is the best character Koontz ever made. The novel is a chase, a love story and a warning about genetic meddling.

name: Clive Barker
teaser: The horror writer who wanted to be the next William Blake — his Books of Blood (1984) announced a new voice in horror, and his Hellraiser films came from his own novella The Hellbound Heart. He writes horror as dark fantasy, lush and philosophical, and has also directed films and painted. His Imajica is a portal fantasy of staggering invention. Stephen King called him 'the future of horror'.

exploreAction.targetName: The Hellbound Heart and the Books of Blood
exploreAction.instruction: Read The Hellbound Heart — the novella that became Hellraiser — and notice the beauty inside the horror. Barker's monsters are always after something philosophical.

name: Washington Irving
teaser: The father of American literature — Rip Van Winkle and The Legend of Sleepy Hollow gave the young United States its first enduring myths, published in 1819. He invented the American short story, the American humorous essay, and the pen name 'Diedrich Knickerbocker'. He was America's first international literary celebrity, feted in London and Madrid. His history of New York invented a comic past for the city.

exploreAction.targetName: Rip Van Winkle and The Legend of Sleepy Hollow
exploreAction.instruction: Read Rip Van Winkle and notice the politics hidden in the sleep — Rip sleeps through the Revolution and wakes in a country he doesn't recognize. Irving made the American myth and the American joke at once.

name: James Fenimore Cooper
teaser: The first great American novelist — The Last of the Mohicans (1826) invented the frontier adventure and the character of the scout, Natty Bumppo. He wrote the Leatherstocking Tales to give America a past, and in doing so created the Western. Mark Twain hated his prose and wrote a famous parody; generations of readers loved him anyway. He also wrote The Pilot, founding the sea novel.

exploreAction.targetName: The Last of the Mohicans — the novel that invented the frontier
exploreAction.instruction: Read the chase through the wilderness — Cooper's action set-pieces are the DNA of every Western and action movie. Then read Twain's 'Fenimore Cooper's Literary Offenses' for the funniest literary takedown ever.

name: William Dean Howells
teaser: The dean of American letters — as editor of the Atlantic Monthly and Harper's, he championed realism when America wanted romance, publishing Twain, James and Crane. His own novels, The Rise of Silas Lapham and A Hazard of New Fortunes, are quiet masterpieces about money and conscience. He defined 'the American novel' for a generation and fought for realism as a moral duty.

exploreAction.targetName: The Rise of Silas Lapham — the novel of the self-made man
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening and watch Howells build a businessman from the inside — he was the first American novelist to take money seriously as a subject.

name: Stephen Crane
teaser: The boy wonder of American letters — The Red Badge of Courage, written when he was 23 and had never seen a battle, is the great novel of the Civil War, told from inside a soldier's fear. He was a war correspondent, a poet and a short-story writer who died of tuberculosis at 28. His story 'The Open Boat' is the finest account of shipwreck in English, based on his own experience of being shipwrecked.

exploreAction.targetName: The Red Badge of Courage — the novel of fear in battle
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first chapter and feel the dread before the battle — Crane wrote the psychology of war without ever having seen one. Then 'The Open Boat', where the sea is the subject.

name: Thomas Wolfe
teaser: The giant of American autobiography — Look Homeward, Angel (1929) poured his North Carolina childhood into a novel so enormous his editor had to cut it in half. You Can't Go Home Again gave the title phrase to American speech. He wrote in a flood, revised in a flood, and died at 37 of tuberculosis. His prose is huge, hungry and romantic; Faulkner called him the greatest talent of their generation.

exploreAction.targetName: Look Homeward, Angel — the novel of the boy who must leave
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening — Wolfe's prose is an appetite, and the book is a feast. Then the last pages, where the hero walks away from the mountain town that made him.

name: Joseph Heller
teaser: The author of Catch-22 — the novel whose title became a phrase, a logic trap, and a diagnosis of bureaucracy. Published in 1961, it made war absurd and absurdity a literary mode. Heller was a bombardier in World War II; his novel took seven years and nearly broke him. His later novels never matched it, but one book of this rank is a life's work.

exploreAction.targetName: Catch-22 — the novel that named the trap
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first chapters and let the repetitions pile up — the book is built like the trap it describes. The phrase 'catch-22' never appears in the book; the logic does.

name: Richard Ford
teaser: The chronicler of the American West and its men — his Frank Bascombe novels (The Sportswriter, Independence Day, The Lay of the Land, Let Me Be Frank With You) follow a real-estate agent through middle age with a prose of almost unbearable patience. Independence Day won the Pulitzer. His short stories are considered among the best of his generation. He edited The Granta Book of the American Short Story.

exploreAction.targetName: Independence Day — the novel of the American ordinary
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening and surrender to Bascombe's voice — Ford's genius is making a man talking to himself as gripping as any plot.

name: Jane Smiley
teaser: The novelist of American farms, horses and families — A Thousand Acres (1991), her King Lear retelling set on an Iowa farm, won the Pulitzer. Her history of American fiction, and her novel of the equestrian world, Horse Heaven, show a mind that takes huge subjects seriously. She writes with a sociologist's curiosity and a novelist's warmth. Her Moo is a campus satire with a pig at its center.

exploreAction.targetName: A Thousand Acres — King Lear on an Iowa farm
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first chapters and feel the farm — Smiley makes the land a character. Then watch the Lear story arrive in the tractor sheds and county dinners.

name: Sei Shōnagon
teaser: The court lady who invented the list — her Pillow Book, written around 1000 AD in Heian Japan, is a collection of lists ('Things that make one's heart beat faster'), observations, and gossip from the imperial court. It is one of the first great works of women's writing, playful, sharp and entirely personal. She served Empress Teishi and recorded her world with an eye that misses nothing.

exploreAction.targetName: The Pillow Book — the world's first great list-maker
exploreAction.instruction: Read the lists — 'Hateful Things', 'Splendid Things' — and feel the intimacy of a woman writing for herself a thousand years ago. Her voice is modern because it never tries to be.

name: The Brothers Grimm
teaser: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm collected German folk tales to save them from extinction — their Household Tales (1812) gave us Cinderella, Snow White, Rapunzel and Hansel and Gretel. The original versions are darker than the Disney retellings: the evil stepsisters' eyes are pecked out, the witch is burned. They were also pioneering linguists; Jacob's law of sound change is the foundation of historical linguistics.

exploreAction.targetName: Grimm's Fairy Tales — the stories before Disney
exploreAction.instruction: Read the originals and notice what Disney removed — the violence is the point, a warning system for children in a dangerous world. Then read their introduction, the manifesto of folk tale collecting.

name: Heinrich Heine
teaser: The German poet of wit and exile — 'Die Lorelei' and his love lyrics were set to music by Schumann and Schubert; his prose made German satire sing. He converted from Judaism to Christianity, called it his 'ticket into European culture', and was mocked for it. His health collapsed and he spent his last eight years in a 'mattress grave' in Paris, still writing. The Nazis banned his books; the Lorelei was attributed to 'unknown'.

exploreAction.targetName: The poems and prose of Heinrich Heine
exploreAction.instruction: Read 'Die Lorelei' — the poem of the siren on the Rhine — then his letters from the mattress grave, where the wit never dies even as the body does.

name: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
teaser: The philosopher who made modern feeling — his Confessions invented the memoir as self-examination; his Social Contract gave the French Revolution its slogan ('Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains'); his Emile rethought childhood. He was a Geneva watchmaker's son who became the most controversial thinker of the Enlightenment, turning against his own friends. He died in 1778; his ideas helped light 1789.

exploreAction.targetName: The Social Contract and the Confessions
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of the Social Contract, then the first page of the Confessions — 'I have resolved on an enterprise that has no precedent'. Rousseau invented the modern self, and it is him.

name: Jean Racine
teaser: The greatest of French tragedians — Phèdre, Andromaque and Britannicus compress Greek myth into verse of terrifying precision, where a woman's confession of love is also her death sentence. He was Louis XIV's favorite playwright, retired at the height of his fame to become royal historiographer, and wrote only two more plays after the age of 40. French actors still learn their craft on his alexandrines.

exploreAction.targetName: Phèdre — the tragedy of the queen who loves her stepson
exploreAction.instruction: Read Phèdre's confession scene — Racine's alexandrines are the most controlled expression of uncontrollable feeling ever written. Every line is a trap closing.

name: Mme de La Fayette
teaser: The author of The Princess of Cleves (1678), often called the first modern novel — a court lady's story of marriage, duty and a love she refuses, told with psychological precision that feels centuries ahead of its time. Published anonymously, it scandalized and fascinated Versailles. La Fayette was a confidante of the court and wrote her masterpiece from inside the world it describes.

exploreAction.targetName: The Princess of Cleves — the first modern novel
exploreAction.instruction: Read the scene where the princess confesses her love to her husband — a scene no one had written before, of unbearable honesty. The novel's restraint is its power.

name: Alain Robbe-Grillet
teaser: The theorist of the nouveau roman — his novels (The Erasers, Jealousy, In the Labyrinth) describe objects with obsessive precision and people barely at all. His manifesto 'For a New Novel' declared that plot, character and psychology were obsolete. He also wrote the screenplay for Last Year at Marienbad. Dense, experimental and controversial, he was the most argued-about French novelist of the 1950s and 60s.

exploreAction.targetName: Jealousy — the novel of the watching husband
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening and notice what is described — a table, a terrace, a banana tree — and what is not: the wife's affair is built entirely from the arrangement of objects.

name: Alexander Solzhenitsyn
teaser: The writer who broke the silence of the Gulag — One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich (1962) described a single day in a Soviet labor camp with such plainness that it was allowed to be published, then banned. The Gulag Archipelago, his massive history of the camp system, cost him his citizenship. He won the Nobel in 1970, was exiled in 1974, returned after the USSR fell, and became a prophet of Russia's suffering.

exploreAction.targetName: One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich — one day in the Gulag
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first hours of the day — the cold, the bread, the count — and feel how one ordinary day contains the whole system. Solzhenitsyn's plainness is the most powerful weapon he had.

name: Andrei Bely
teaser: The symbolist novelist whose Petersburg (1913) is often called the most important Russian novel of the century after Ulysses — a city, a family and a bomb plot told in prose that shimmers between verse and music. Bely was also a poet and critic who influenced everyone from Nabokov to the Futurists. Petersburg is difficult, gorgeous and prophetic: the city itself is the protagonist.

exploreAction.targetName: Petersburg — the novel of the city as a nervous system
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening and let the prose wash over you — Bely's sentences are musical. The plot is a bomb, but the book is about the city's fever.

name: Maxim Gorky
teaser: The founder of socialist realism and the voice of the Russian poor — his memoir trilogy (Childhood, In the World, My Universities) is the great autobiography of poverty. He rose from orphanhood and wandering to be Lenin's friend and the Soviet Union's literary patron; his later enthusiasm for the regime that crushed his countrymen is the tragedy of his life. His play The Lower Depths is a masterpiece of the dispossessed.

exploreAction.targetName: My Childhood — the autobiography of poverty
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first chapters and meet the grandfather whose violence shaped Gorky — the memoir is the origin story of the revolution's favorite writer, and it is anything but propaganda.

name: Vasily Grossman
teaser: The chronicler of the Holocaust and the Soviet war — Life and Fate, his novel of the Battle of Stalingrad, was seized by the KGB in 1961 and smuggled out; it is often called the Soviet War and Peace. He was a war correspondent who filed the first eyewitness report of a Nazi extermination camp. His Everything Flows, written in secret at the end of his life, indicts the Soviet system itself.

exploreAction.targetName: Life and Fate — the Soviet War and Peace
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters set in Stalingrad — Grossman writes war as a physical fact. Then the sections in the German camp, where the novel becomes a meditation on evil.

name: Miguel de Unamuno
teaser: The Spanish existentialist before existentialism — his Tragic Sense of Life argues that the hunger for immortality is the core of human feeling, and that reason cannot satisfy it. His novel Mist (Niebla) has the protagonist argue with his author about whether he exists. He was a Basque rector of Salamanca, exiled by the dictator Primo de Rivera, and his 'I do not want to die' defined the Spanish temperament in philosophy.

exploreAction.targetName: Mist — the novel where the character argues with his author
exploreAction.instruction: Read the moment when Augusto discovers he is a character — the conversation with Unamuno is the most dizzying scene in Spanish fiction.

name: Gabriela Mistral
teaser: The first Latin American to win the Nobel Prize in Literature (1945) — a Chilean poet of motherhood, grief and the landscape, writing in a voice of elemental simplicity.
