Feist wrote his first novel in 1977 and went on to build the Riftwar Cycle of 30 books. He wrote with warmth and momentum, and his novels sold millions worldwide.

exploreAction.targetName: Magician — the novel of the apprentice and the warrior
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first chapters in Crydee — the raid that changes everything comes early. Feist's two-protagonist structure (Pug and Tomas) gives the reader two books in one.

name: Tad Williams
teaser: The author of Memory, Sorrow, and Thorn — the fantasy trilogy (begun 1988) that inspired George R.R. Martin's approach to epic fantasy, with its realistic politics and slow-burn quest. Williams's Otherland series was an early portal to the virtual world, and his epic of the dragon Osten Ard, The Last King of Osten Ard, continues the story decades later. He is a master of the long, immersive series.

exploreAction.targetName: The Dragonbone Chair — the first book of Memory, Sorrow, and Thorn
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening in the castle of Hayholt — Williams takes his time, and the slow start is the point. Martin has said this trilogy was a direct influence on A Song of Ice and Fire.

name: Guy Gavriel Kay
teaser: The Canadian fantasy writer of 'history with a quarter-turn to the fantastic' — Tigana, The Lions of Al-Rassan and Under Heaven are set in worlds that are clearly Renaissance Italy, Moorish Spain and Tang China, with one magical twist. He worked on the Silmarillion with Christopher Tolkien, and his prose is considered the finest in modern fantasy. His books are beloved for their beauty and their grief.

exploreAction.targetName: Tigana — the novel of the erased name
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening and feel the magic — a sorcerer has erased the name of a country so no one can speak it. The novel is about memory, music and revenge, and its ending is devastating.

name: Joe Abercrombie
teaser: The British writer of 'grimdark' fantasy — The First Law trilogy (begun 2006) features torturers, cripples and cynical kings, and is the most acclaimed example of the subgenre he helped define. He was a film editor before writing, which shows in his set pieces. His characters — Logen Ninefingers, Glokta the torturer — are memorably awful and beloved. His later Age of Madness trilogy confirmed he is the genre's sharpest wit.

exploreAction.targetName: The Blade Itself — the first book of the First Law
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first chapters and meet Glokta, the crippled torturer who is the most sympathetic character in the book — Abercrombie's moral inversion is the whole point. The trilogy's ending is a masterpiece of anticlimax.

name: Steven Erikson
teaser: The author of the Malazan Book of the Fallen — ten volumes of epic fantasy (begun 1999) with a cast of hundreds, an archaeologist's eye for civilization, and no hand-holding for the reader. He was an archaeologist and anthropologist in Canada, which shows in his treatment of history, war and empire. His novels are dense, brutal and rewarding, and his fan community is famously devoted. He also writes crime fiction with Ian Cameron Esslemont.

exploreAction.targetName: Gardens of the Moon — the first book of the Malazan Book of the Fallen
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening and surrender to the immersion — Erikson drops you into a war and a magic system without explanation. The series is the most ambitious epic fantasy ever attempted.

name: Roger Zelazny
teaser: The science fantasy writer of Lord of Light and the Amber series — he won the Hugo six times and the Nebula three, and his prose is the most poetic in the genre's history. Lord of Light (1967) tells of men who seized godhood in a Hindu-inspired world; Nine Princes in Amber (1970) begins the series about a royal family who can walk between parallel worlds. He died in 1995 at 58, and his work influenced everything from Sandman to The Matrix.

exploreAction.targetName: Lord of Light — the novel of the false gods
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first chapter and surrender to the style — Zelazny's language is fire. The novel's Buddhism and gunfights and god-war made it the most influential SF novel of its decade.

name: Gene Wolfe
teaser: The writer SF critics call the greatest living author in the genre — his Book of the New Sun (1980-83) is a masterpiece narrated by an unreliable torturer's apprentice in a far-future dying Earth. Wolfe's work rewards re-reading: every narration hides a different truth. He was an engineer who edited Plant Engineering magazine and wrote fiction at night. He won the World Fantasy Award for lifetime achievement and is often compared to Borges.

exploreAction.targetName: The Shadow of the Torturer — the first book of the New Sun
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first chapters and distrust the narrator — Severian claims to remember everything, which is the clue. Wolfe's prose is beautiful and his puzzles are infinite; the series is the most rewarding in SF.

name: Harlan Ellison
teaser: The angry man of science fiction — his short stories ('I Have No Mouth, and I Must Scream', 'A Boy and His Dog', 'Repent, Harlequin!') won more awards than almost any writer's, and his essays and feuds were legendary. He wrote the classic Star Trek episode 'The City on the Edge of Forever'. He was brilliant, belligerent and prolific, publishing over 1,700 stories. He died in 2018, still the genre's most quoted contrarian.

exploreAction.targetName: I Have No Mouth, and I Must Scream — the stories of Harlan Ellison
exploreAction.instruction: Read the title story — five people trapped inside a murderous supercomputer for eternity. Ellison's darkness is the point: the genre's angriest writer made its most unforgiving stories.

name: Alfred Bester
teaser: The writer who showed science fiction what style could be — his The Demolished Man (1953), about a murder in a world of telepaths, won the first Hugo Award, and The Stars My Destination (1956) is a revenge epic often called the genre's best novel. He was a comic book writer and radio scriptwriter who brought pace and punch to SF. He stopped writing SF for decades, and returned in the 70s. His influence on cyberpunk is acknowledged by Gibson himself.

exploreAction.targetName: The Stars My Destination — the novel of the revenge of Gully Foyle
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening — Gully Foyle, a common sailor, survives a wreck alone and vows revenge on the ship that passed him by. Bester's pyrotechnic style is the genre's most exhilarating read.

name: Olaf Stapledon
teaser: The philosopher of science fiction — Last and First Men (1930) tells the entire future history of humanity across two billion years and 18 species; Star Maker (1937) goes further, to the birth of the cosmos. He was a Liverpool philosopher who wrote SF as thought experiments, and his scale made him the genre's only true visionary of the deep time. Arthur C. Clarke called Star Maker the greatest work of imagination ever written.

exploreAction.targetName: Star Maker — the novel of the creation of the universe
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening — a man gazes at the stars and his mind detaches to travel through space. Stapledon's novel encompasses every civilization, and the 'Star Maker' of the title is the book's final revelation.

name: Mervyn Peake
teaser: The author of the Gormenghast trilogy — Titus Groan (1946) and Gormenghast (1950) are a gothic masterpiece set in a vast castle of ritual and decay, written in prose of extraordinary richness. Peake was also a painter and war artist who drew the Blitz; his novels are the strangest classics in English fantasy. He died in 1968 of a neurological disease, leaving the trilogy unfinished. His influence runs from Moorcock to the present.

exploreAction.targetName: Titus Groan — the novel of the castle of Gormenghast
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first chapters and feel the castle — Peake's Gormenghast is a character, a machine of ritual in which the infant Titus is born. The prose is the most ornate in fantasy, and it is worth every word.

name: Madeleine L'Engle
teaser: The author of A Wrinkle in Time (1962) — the Newbery-winning novel of Meg Murry traveling through space-time to rescue her father, which was rejected by 26 publishers and is now a classic and a film. L'Engle wrote science fantasy rooted in Christian faith and family love. She published more than 60 books, including the rest of the Time Quintet. Her journals and essays about writing are beloved by writers.

exploreAction.targetName: A Wrinkle in Time — the novel of the tesseract
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first chapters and meet Meg — the awkward girl who saves the universe by loving. L'Engle's novel made quantum physics a children's adventure and changed children's literature.

name: Beatrix Potter
teaser: The author and illustrator of The Tale of Peter Rabbit (1902) — the best-selling children's book of all time, written as a picture letter to a sick child. Potter was a naturalist who drew fungi and sheep, and her picture letters became the first books to combine text and image perfectly. She bought a farm in the Lake District with her royalties and became a prize-winning sheep breeder and conservationist. She died in 1943, leaving her land to the National Trust.

exploreAction.targetName: The Tale of Peter Rabbit — the picture letter that became a classic
exploreAction.instruction: Read it as a picture letter — the book began as a letter to a five-year-old. Potter's economy (text and image on every page) invented the modern picture book.

name: Michael Ende
teaser: The German author of The Neverending Story (1979) — the novel of a boy who reads a book that reads back, which became a global phenomenon and a film. Ende wrote fantasy with philosophical depth; Momo (1973), about a girl who fights the time thieves, is his other masterpiece. He disliked the film adaptation of his book, and his work is a quiet rebellion against the modern worship of efficiency. He died in 1995.

exploreAction.targetName: The Neverending Story — the novel of the book that reads back
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening — Bastian steals into a bookshop and opens a book printed in two colors, and the reader's own reading becomes the plot. Ende's novel is about the imagination's survival.

name: Michael Moorcock
teaser: The British writer who modernized fantasy — his Elric of Melniboné (the albino emperor with the soul-stealing sword) and the Eternal Champion cycle made him the most influential fantasy writer of the 60s and 70s. He was also the editor of New Worlds magazine, where he published the New Wave of SF. He is a musician who played in the band Hawkwind. He has won the Nebula and the World Fantasy lifetime award, and his influence is everywhere in modern fantasy.

exploreAction.targetName: Elric of Melniboné — the novel of the albino emperor
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first chapters and meet Elric — the sickly albino who wields the demonic sword Stormbringer. Moorcock's anti-hero invented the morally grey fantasy protagonist decades before the term existed.

name: Robert E. Howard
teaser: The creator of Conan the Barbarian — his pulp fiction of the 1930s invented sword and sorcery, and his death at 30 by suicide cut short one of the most original voices in popular fiction. He wrote thousands of pages of adventure, horror and history, set in his invented Hyborian Age. Conan's first appearance, 'The Phoenix on the Sword', appeared in Weird Tales in 1932. His other creations include Solomon Kane and Kull. He wrote from Cross Plains, Texas, his whole life.

exploreAction.targetName: The Phoenix on the Sword and the Conan stories
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first Conan story — 'The Phoenix on the Sword' — and feel the genre being born. Howard's prose is a charge of adrenaline, and his Conan is far more than the film versions.

name: Ross Macdonald
teaser: The psychological detective novelist — his Lew Archer novels (The Galton Case, The Chill) turned the hard-boiled form toward family secrets and California's past, and are considered by many critics the finest American detective fiction. He was a Canadian who worked as a social worker, which shaped his sympathy. His plots are dense with buried history; his style is lean and precise. He died in 1983, praised by Faulkner and Camus.

exploreAction.targetName: The Galton Case — the novel of the missing heir
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening and meet Lew Archer — the detective who listens. Macdonald's theme is that the past is never buried, and his California is a landscape of secrets.

name: James M. Cain
teaser: The author of The Postman Always Rings Twice (1934) and Double Indemnity — the twin peaks of noir, both made into classic films. Cain was a journalist and screenwriter whose novels of murder, money and desire are short, brutal and perfect. He wrote about ordinary people who kill, and his prose is stripped to the bone. He died in 1977, and his novels are the purest American noir.

exploreAction.targetName: The Postman Always Rings Twice — the novel of the drifter and the wife
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first chapter and feel the heat — the drifter and the wife of the diner owner are doomed from page one. Cain's novel is 120 pages of perfect tension, and the films made it famous.

name: Ruth Rendell
teaser: The British crime writer who won four Edgars and the Diamond Dagger — her Inspector Wexford series (From Doon with Death, 1964) ran for 50 years, and her psychological thrillers under her own name are among the darkest in the genre. As Barbara Vine she wrote the psychological masterpiece A Favor for a Child. She was made a life peer and served in the House of Lords. She died in 2015, leaving 70 novels of unease.

exploreAction.targetName: From Doon with Death — the first Wexford novel
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first chapters and meet Inspector Wexford — Rendell's series began with a missing housewife and ran half a century. Her psychological novels are darker and stranger than the series.

name: P.D. James
teaser: The queen of British crime — her Adam Dalgliesh novels (Cover Her Face, 1962) and her standalone thrillers (Innocent Blood, The Children of Men) are crime fiction as literature. She worked in the NHS and the Home Office before writing full time, and was made a life peer. She wrote about evil with theological seriousness and prose of great control. She published her last novel at 88 and died in 2014 at 94.

exploreAction.targetName: The Children of Men — the novel of the sterile future
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening — humanity has been sterile for 25 years, and the last generation is aging out. James's dystopia is quiet, English and devastating, and the film adaptation changed its ending.

name: Colin Dexter
teaser: The creator of Inspector Morse — the Oxford detective whose novels (Last Bus to Woodstock, 1975) and the long-running TV series made him a national treasure. Dexter was a classics teacher who wrote crossword puzzles before novels; Morse's love of opera, beer and cryptic clues reflects his creator. He won two Edgars and the Diamond Dagger, and died in 2017. His last Morse novel was published in 1999, the year before the series ended.

exploreAction.targetName: Last Bus to Woodstock — the first Morse novel
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first chapters and meet Morse in Oxford — the detective who solves puzzles in a city of them. Dexter's crossword structure (every clue matters) is the series' signature.

name: Ian Rankin
teaser: Scotland's crime novelist — his Inspector Rebus series (Knots and Crosses, 1987) has run for 30 years and made Edinburgh a crime fiction capital. Rankin was a PhD student who wrote songs before novels; Rebus is a flawed, whisky-drinking detective in the Chandler tradition. He has won the Edgar, the Diamond Dagger and the CWA's Cartier Diamond Dagger. He was made an OBE and now lives between Edinburgh and London.

exploreAction.targetName: Knots and Crosses — the first Rebus novel
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first chapters and meet John Rebus in Edinburgh — the detective with a past he can't escape. Rankin's series has aged its hero in real time, and Rebus is one of crime fiction's great characters.

name: Tana French
teaser: The Irish crime novelist of the Dublin Murder Squad — In the Woods (2007) won the Edgar for best first novel, and her books (The Likeness, Broken Harbor, The Trespasser) follow detectives who are as damaged as the cases. She trained as an actor at Trinity College Dublin before writing. Her prose is literary, her police are human, and her Dublin is a character. She is the most acclaimed crime writer of her generation.

exploreAction.targetName: In the Woods — the novel of the detective and his past
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first chapters and meet Rob Ryan — the detective whose childhood trauma returns with the case. French's novel is a police procedural that is also a novel of memory, and it changed Irish crime fiction.

name: Dennis Lehane
teaser: The American crime novelist of Mystic River, Gone Baby Gone and Shutter Island — all filmed, all set in his native Boston. He began with the Kenzie-Gennaro private eye series and became a literary novelist who happens to write crime. He also wrote for The Wire and Boardwalk Empire. His prose is tough and tender at once, and his sense of place (Boston's working class) is the best in the genre. He lives in California now.

exploreAction.targetName: Mystic River — the novel of the three childhood friends
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first chapters and feel Boston — the three boys' childhood trauma comes home with a murder. Lehane's novel is a tragedy disguised as a mystery, and the film with Sean Penn kept its power.

name: Michael Connelly
teaser: The best-selling crime novelist of the modern era — his Harry Bosch series (The Black Echo, 1992) and the Lincoln Lawyer series have sold 80 million copies and become TV shows. Connelly was a crime reporter in Los Angeles, which gives his police procedurals their authenticity. Bosch is named for Hieronymus Bosch and is as relentless as the painter's hells. Connelly has won the Edgar four times and is the genre's most reliable master.

exploreAction.targetName: The Black Echo — the first Harry Bosch novel
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first chapters and meet Harry Bosch — the LAPD detective who follows the case into the tunnels and the past. Connelly's procedural detail is the genre's gold standard.

name: Lee Child
teaser: The creator of Jack Reacher — the drifter who wanders America righting wrongs, who debuted in Killing Floor (1997) and has appeared in 28 novels, selling 100 million copies. Child was a British television director who was laid off and wrote the first Reacher book in two weeks. Reacher is a hobo knight: no phone, no home, one toothbrush. Tom Cruise played him in two films; Alan Ritchson plays him in the TV series. Child handed the series to his brother Andrew in 2020.

exploreAction.targetName: Killing Floor — the first Jack Reacher novel
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first chapters and meet Reacher in Margrave, Georgia — the drifter who arrives in a town and finds a body. Child's formula (Reacher arrives, trouble follows, justice happens) is the most successful in thriller fiction.

name: John Grisham
teaser: The legal thriller writer who sold 300 million copies — A Time to Kill (1989), The Firm (1991) and The Pelican Brief made the courtroom a bestseller. Grisham was a Mississippi lawyer and state legislator who wrote his first novel at dawn before work. His books have been adapted into dozens of films. He also writes baseball fiction and Christmas stories. He is the best-selling American novelist of his generation.

exploreAction.targetName: The Firm — the novel of the young lawyer in danger
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first chapters and meet Mitch McDeere — the Harvard law graduate who takes the job that will trap him. Grisham's novel made the legal thriller the genre of the 90s.

name: Gillian Flynn
teaser: The author of Gone Girl (2012) — the psychological thriller that became a phenomenon, a film and a cultural reset for the genre. She was a television critic who wrote crime novels at night; her first two books (Sharp Objects, Dark Places) preceded the smash. Her work is known for its unreliable narrators and its fury. She has written screenplays, including the adaptation of Gone Girl directed by David Fincher. She is the most influential thriller writer of her decade.

exploreAction.targetName: Gone Girl — the novel of the missing wife
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first chapters and trust nothing — Flynn's split-narrative (the husband's diary, the wife's journal) is a machine for misdirection. The twist is the book's engine, and the ending is the argument.

name: Jo Nesbø
teaser: Norway's crime king — his Harry Hole series (The Redbreast, The Snowman, Knife) has sold 55 million copies, and his standalone thriller Headhunters became a hit film. Nesbø was a footballer, a rock musician and an economist before writing; he has kept playing music with his band Di Derre. Hole is a brilliant, self-destructive detective in the classic mold. Nesbø also writes children's books about Doctor Proctor. He is the most successful Norwegian author since Ibsen.

exploreAction.targetName: The Snowman — the novel of the serial killer
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first chapters and feel the Oslo winter — Nesbø's Harry Hole is the most damaged great detective in crime fiction. The Snowman is the series' most famous entry and its most chilling.

name: Georges Simenon
teaser: The Belgian creator of Inspector Maigret — 75 novels and 28 short stories about the pipe-smoking Paris detective, making him the most translated francophone author ever. Simenon wrote with extraordinary speed (a Maigret in a week) and also wrote 400 psychological novels under his own name. He said he wrote to understand people, not to solve crimes. He died in 1989 at 86, having written 400 million copies' worth of books.

exploreAction.targetName: The Maigret novels — the detective of understanding
exploreAction.instruction: Read Pietr the Latvian, the first Maigret novel — Simenon's detective solves by empathy, not deduction. The books are short, atmospheric and the most humane in crime fiction.

name: Ken Follett
teaser: The Welsh novelist of the epic — The Pillars of the Earth (1989), about the building of a cathedral in 12th-century England, sold 27 million copies and spawned sequels and a video game. He began with thrillers (Eye of the Needle, 1978) and moved to history with a thriller's engine. His Century Trilogy covers the 20th century in three novels. He is one of the best-selling novelists in the world, with 178 million copies sold.

exploreAction.targetName: The Pillars of the Earth — the novel of the cathedral
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first chapters and feel the medieval world — Follett's cathedral builders are heroes, villains and lovers in a story that took him three years to research. The book made historical fiction a bestseller genre again.

name: Robert Ludlum
teaser: The thriller writer of the Bourne novels — The Bourne Identity (1980), about an amnesiac assassin, became the film franchise with Matt Damon. Ludlum was an actor and producer who wrote his first novel at 43. His books — The Osterman Weekend, The Chancellor Manuscript — sold over 300 million copies, and his formula (the lone operative against the conspiracy) defined the modern thriller. He died in 2001; the Bourne series continues with other writers.

exploreAction.targetName: The Bourne Identity — the novel of the man without a memory
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first chapters and meet the man pulled from the sea — Ludlum's amnesiac agent is the modern thriller's founding character. The films are faster; the book is denser and darker.

name: Tom Clancy
teaser: The author of The Hunt for Red October (1984) — the submarine thriller that made him the best-selling thriller writer in America. Clancy was an insurance salesman who wrote military techno-thrillers with obsessive technical detail; his Jack Ryan novels (Patriot Games, Clear and Present Danger) defined the genre and the films. He also founded the video game series Rainbow Six and Splinter Cell. He died in 2013, having sold over 100 million books.

exploreAction.targetName: The Hunt for Red October — the novel of the submarine
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first chapters and feel the machinery — Clancy's novel of a Soviet submarine captain defecting is a technical manual that happens to be a thriller. The film with Sean Connery is a classic.

name: Louise Glück
teaser: The poet who won the Nobel Prize in 2020 — her work (The Wild Iris, Ararat, Meadowlands) retells myth and family with a spare, devastating voice. She began as a precocious teenager in workshops, struggled with anorexia, and made her illness into her material. She taught at Yale and was Poet Laureate of the United States. The Wild Iris, her book of poems spoken to and by God, is her masterpiece. She died in 2023.

exploreAction.targetName: The Wild Iris — the poems of Louise Glück
exploreAction.instruction: Read the sequence in The Wild Iris — flowers speak to God, God answers, and the garden becomes theology. Glück's plainness is the hardest-won style in modern poetry.

name: Sharon Olds
teaser: The poet of the body — her poems about her parents, her children and her own flesh ('The Dead and the Living') made confessional poetry visceral and won the Pulitzer for Stag's Leap, her book about her divorce. She was New York State Poet Laureate and founded the creative writing program at NYU. Her frankness about family and sex scandalized and liberated readers. She is the most direct poet of her generation.

exploreAction.targetName: Stag's Leap — the poems of the divorce
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening poems of Stag's Leap — the divorce told from the wife's side, with the title as the animal metaphor. Olds's honesty is total, and the Pulitzer committee agreed.

name: Billy Collins
teaser: The most popular American poet of his generation — as Poet Laureate 2001-03, he made poetry approachable with his funny, conversational poems ('Introduction to Poetry', 'The Lanyard'). He hosts the Poetry 180 program for schools and has sold more poetry books than almost any living poet. Critics sometimes sniff; readers keep buying. His poems are the doorway into poetry for millions.

exploreAction.targetName: Sailing Alone Around the Room — the poems of Billy Collins
exploreAction.instruction: Read 'Introduction to Poetry' — the poem about how readers should not torture poems. Then 'The Lanyard', where a mother's gift of a lanyard outweighs all gratitude. Collins's lightness hides real depth.

name: John Ashbery
teaser: The most influential American poet of the late century — his Self-Portrait in a Convex Mirror (1975) won all three major prizes, and his long, drifting, collage-like poems ('Flow Chart') redefined what a poem could be. He was also an art critic for New York magazine. His poems are notoriously difficult and secretly funny; he said he wanted his poems to be 'as fresh and surprising as a dream'. He died in 2017, the elder statesman of the avant-garde.

exploreAction.targetName: Self-Portrait in a Convex Mirror — the poems of John Ashbery
exploreAction.instruction: Read the title poem — a meditation on a Parmigianino painting that becomes a meditation on consciousness. Ashbery's sentences wander into meaning like water finding its level.

name: Frank O'Hara
teaser: The poet of New York and of the everyday — his 'I do this, I do that' poems ('Having a Coke with You', 'The Day Lady Died') treat lunch, movies and friends as material for art. He worked as a curator at MoMA and was the center of the New York School. He was killed at 40, run over by a dune buggy on Fire Island. His Lunch Poems (1964) remain the most alive poetry of the mid-century.

exploreAction.targetName: Lunch Poems — the poems of Frank O'Hara
exploreAction.instruction: Read 'The Day Lady Died' — the poem of a lunch hour that ends with the news of Billie Holiday's death. O'Hara's casualness is the art; the poem is a walk through New York that becomes an elegy.

name: Allen Ginsberg
teaser: The poet of Howl (1956) — the poem that was put on trial for obscenity and won, freeing American literature. Ginsberg was the bard of the Beats, the friend of Kerouac and Burroughs, a Buddhist and a gay pioneer who wrote 'A Supermarket in California' and 'Kaddish', his elegy for his mother. He read at the 1967 Human Be-In, marched against the war, and remained America's public poet until his death in 1997.

exploreAction.targetName: Howl and Other Poems — the poem that won its trial
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first section of Howl aloud — 'I saw the best minds of my generation destroyed by madness' — then read about the obscenity trial that made the poem a landmark of free speech.

name: William S. Burroughs
teaser: The cut-up writer of Naked Lunch (1959) — the novel that survived its own obscenity trial and became the Beat Generation's dark bible. Burroughs was a Harvard heir, a heroin addict, and an accidental killer (he shot his wife in a William Tell game in Mexico City). His cut-up method — slicing texts and rearranging — influenced everyone from the Beatles to David Bowie. He was the most dangerous mind of the Beats and died in 1997.

exploreAction.targetName: Naked Lunch — the novel of the virus
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening and surrender — Burroughs's novel has no plot, only a fever of addiction, control and horror. The obscenity trial that followed its publication is a landmark of free expression.

name: Joan Didion
teaser: The essayist of California and of grief — her Slouching Towards Bethlehem (1968) defined New Journalism, and The Year of Magical Thinking (2005), about the sudden death of her husband, won the National Book Award. She wrote about the counterculture, the Manson murders, and her own collapse with a cool that became the model of American prose. She died in 2021; her sunglasses are now in a museum.

exploreAction.targetName: The Year of Magical Thinking — the memoir of grief
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening pages — Didion describes the ordinary moment her husband died, and the magical thinking that followed. The book is grief made prose, and it won every prize.

name: Susan Sontag
teaser: The intellectual of the image — her Against Interpretation (1966), On Photography (1977) and Illness as Metaphor (1978) changed how we think about art, cameras and disease. She wrote novels too, and her essay on the Iraq war, 'Regarding the Torture of Others', was a landmark. She was a New York intellectual of the old school, famous and fiercely argued with. She died in 2004 of cancer, which she wrote about in Illness as Metaphor and its sequel.

exploreAction.targetName: On Photography — the book about what cameras do
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first essay — Sontag argues that to photograph is to appropriate, and that photographs have changed the meaning of reality. The book is 50 years old and more true every year.

name: Harriet Beecher Stowe
teaser: The author of Uncle Tom's Cabin (1852) — the novel that Abraham Lincoln reportedly called 'the book that started this great war'. It was the best-selling novel of the 19th century and the most powerful piece of abolitionist propaganda ever written. Stowe was a preacher's daughter and mother of seven who wrote the book in installments. Its title character's name became a slur, a bitter irony for a novel that humanized the enslaved. She died in 1896.

exploreAction.targetName: Uncle Tom's Cabin — the novel that changed a nation
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening and feel the book's power — Stowe's novel made slavery's cruelty vivid to millions of readers. Lincoln's greeting to her in 1862 — 'so this is the little lady who made this big war' — is the most famous author anecdote in American history.

name: Louisa May Alcott
teaser: The author of Little Women (1868) — the novel of the four March sisters that has never been out of print and is a founding text of American girlhood. Alcott wrote it in six weeks at her publisher's request, based on her own family; Jo March is her. She was also a nurse in the Civil War, wrote thrillers under a pen name to pay the bills, and supported her family her whole life. She never married and died in 1888, two days after her father.

exploreAction.targetName: Little Women — the novel of the four sisters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first chapters and meet Meg, Jo, Beth and Amy — Alcott wrote the book in six weeks, and Jo March, the tomboy writer, is the author herself. The sequel, Good Wives, is part of the same volume.

name: Harriet Jacobs
teaser: The author of Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl (1861) — the first autobiography by an enslaved woman in America, published under the pseudonym Linda Brent. Jacobs hid for seven years in a crawlspace above her grandmother's shed to escape her enslaver, then escaped north. Her account of the sexual predation of slavery was doubted by white abolitionists until historians confirmed it. She worked as a nurse and abolitionist in the North.

exploreAction.targetName: Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl — the memoir of the crawlspace
exploreAction.instruction: Read the chapters of the seven years in the garret — Jacobs's account of hiding to save her children is the most harrowing and most necessary American autobiography. She wrote it herself, which was the controversy.

name: Frederick Douglass
teaser: The escaped slave who became the most photographed American of the 19th century — his Narrative (1845) is the great American autobiography, and his speeches ('What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?') are among the most powerful oratory in the language. He taught himself to read against the law, escaped by train, and became an abolitionist, editor and diplomat. He was the most famous Black American of his century and died in 1895.

exploreAction.targetName: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
exploreAction.instruction: Read the chapters on learning to read — the master's wife teaches him, then is forbidden, and Douglass learns anyway from the white boys. The book is freedom made prose.

name: W.E.B. Du Bois
teaser: The scholar who founded Black sociology — The Souls of Black Folk (1903) coined the concept of 'double consciousness' and the phrase 'the color line', and his monumental Black Reconstruction (1935) rewrote the history of the era. He was the first Black man to earn a Harvard PhD, a founder of the NAACP, and the editor of The Crisis. He moved to Ghana at 93 and died there in 1963, the day before the March on Washington.

exploreAction.targetName: The Souls of Black Folk — the book of double consciousness
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first chapters — 'The problem of the twentieth century is the problem of the color line'. Du Bois's prose is the most eloquent in American social thought.

name: Malcolm X
teaser: The Autobiography of Malcolm X (1965), as told to Alex Haley, is one of the great American life stories — from street hustler to Nation of Islam minister to, in his last year, a man who broke with the Nation and was assassinated at 39. The book's ending, written with Haley while the assassins were closing in, is the most moving final chapter in American autobiography. His daughter and the film adaptation by Spike Lee kept the story alive.

exploreAction.targetName: The Autobiography of Malcolm X — the life story
exploreAction.instruction: Read the early chapters of his hustling years in Boston and Harlem — the book's power is the arc: the con man becomes the minister becomes the pilgrim. The final chapter, written days before his death, is unbearable.

name: Martin Luther King Jr.
teaser: The leader of the American civil rights movement — his 'Letter from Birmingham Jail' (1963) and 'I Have a Dream' speech are among the greatest American documents, and his books (Stride Toward Freedom, Where Do We Go from Here) are the movement's theology. He was assassinated in 1968 at 39. His philosophy of nonviolence was rooted in Gandhi and the black church. He was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize at 35, the youngest winner at the time.

exploreAction.targetName: Why We Can't Wait — the book of the Birmingham campaign
exploreAction.instruction: Read the Letter from Birmingham Jail in full — written on the margins of a newspaper in a cell, it answers the clergy who called his protests untimely. The letter is the movement's mind.

name: Arthur Rimbaud
teaser: The prodigy who stopped writing at 20 — Rimbaud wrote all his poetry as a teenager, including 'Le Bateau ivre' (The Drunken Boat) and A Season in Hell, then abandoned literature for gun-running in Africa. He was Verlaine's lover and the subject of the most famous literary scandal of the century (Verlaine shot him in the wrist). He died at 37 of cancer in Marseille. His 'dérèglement de tous les sens' (derangement of all the senses) became the charter of modern poetry.

exploreAction.targetName: A Season in Hell — the memoir of the visionary
exploreAction.instruction: Read 'The Drunken Boat' — the poem of a boat running wild on the seas, written when Rimbaud was 17. Then the prose of A Season in Hell, which he called his 'farewell to literature'.

name: Paul Verlaine
teaser: The poet of music — his Romances sans paroles and Fêtes galantes made poetry almost purely musical, and his affair with Rimbaud and his shooting of him made him notorious. He was a civil servant who drank, served prison time, and wrote some of the most delicate poems in French ('Il pleure dans mon cœur'). He was elected 'Prince of Poets' in 1894. He died in 1896, mourned by the poets he had influenced.

exploreAction.targetName: Romances sans paroles — the poems of Verlaine
exploreAction.instruction: Read 'Il pleure dans mon cœur' — the poem of rain as the heart's weeping. Verlaine's art is suggestion; he said 'music before everything'.

name: Stéphane Mallarmé
teaser: The most hermetic of the French symbolists — his poem 'Un coup de dés' (A Roll of the Dice, 1897) scattered words across the page and is the ancestor of concrete poetry and every experimental text since. He was a schoolteacher who hosted the famous Tuesday salons of Paris. His 'L'Après-midi d'un faune' became Debussy's orchestral prelude. He said poetry was the language reduced to its essential state. He died in 1898.

exploreAction.targetName: Un coup de dés — the poem printed as a constellation
exploreAction.instruction: Read the facsimile of the poem — the type sizes and page layout are the meaning. Mallarmé said the poem was 'a constellation' and it changed typography forever.

name: André Breton
teaser: The pope of surrealism — his Manifesto of Surrealism (1924) defined the movement ('pure psychic automatism'), and his novel Nadja (1928) is the surrealist masterpiece of walking through Paris with a mysterious woman. He was a doctor who treated shell shock in World War I, which convinced him of the unconscious. He quarreled with everyone (he expelled members for political disagreements) and remained the movement's center until his death in 1966.

exploreAction.targetName: Nadja — the novel of the surreal encounter
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening pages and feel the method — Breton describes his walks through Paris and his meeting with Nadja, who may be mad or may be the point. The book is philosophy as a walk.

name: Georges Perec
teaser: The novelist of constraint — his Life: A User's Manual (1978) builds a Paris apartment building through 99 chapters of interlocking stories, and his novel La Disparition (1969) was written entirely without the letter 'e'. He was an orphan of the Holocaust (his parents died in the camps) who turned loss into games. He also wrote the famous 'I remember' lists. He died at 45 in 1982. He is the most playful serious writer of the century.

exploreAction.targetName: Life: A User's Manual — the novel of the building
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first chapters and meet the tenants of 11 Rue Simon-Crubellier — Perec's novel is structured like a knight's tour of a chessboard, and every apartment contains a life. The 'e'-less novel is the same author's impossible feat.

name: Michel de Montaigne
teaser: The inventor of the essay — his Essays (1580) created the form as a way of thinking on the page, and his 'Que sais-je?' ('What do I know?') is the motto of skepticism. He was a French nobleman and mayor of Bordeaux who retired to his tower to write about himself, and in writing about himself he wrote about everyone. His essay 'Of Cannibals' argues that 'barbarians' are not the ones he expected. He died in 1592.

exploreAction.targetName: The Essays of Montaigne — the book of the self
exploreAction.instruction: Read 'Of Cannibals' — Montaigne's argument that the Tupinambá are more civilized than Europeans is the founding document of cultural relativism. Then read any essay; the form is the freedom.

name: Blaise Pascal
teaser: The mathematician-philosopher of the Pensées — his unfinished book of fragments (1670) contains the 'wager' on God's existence and the line 'the heart has its reasons which reason knows nothing of'. He built one of the first calculating machines, pioneered probability, and then had a mystical vision in 1654 that turned him to religion. His Provincial Letters are the first great modern polemic. He died at 39, his Pensées unfinished.

exploreAction.targetName: Pensées — the fragments of Pascal
exploreAction.instruction: Read the fragments in any order — the wager is the most famous: if God exists you gain everything by believing; if not, you lose little. Pascal's mathematics and his faith meet in the fragments.

name: Eugène Ionesco
teaser: The playwright of the absurd — his The Bald Soprano (1950) and Rhinoceros (1959) made nonsense a dramatic form. He was a Romanian who moved to Paris and said his first play was written when he tried to learn English from a phrasebook — the platitudes became the dialogue. Rhinoceros, about a town turning into rhinoceroses, is his allegory of fascism. He was elected to the Académie française, the absurdist who became an institution. He died in 1994.

exploreAction.targetName: Rhinoceros — the play of the town turning into beasts
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first act — one rhinoceros passes, then another, and the townspeople argue about it. Ionesco's allegory of conformity was written after watching his hometown embrace fascism.

name: Kawabata Yasunari
teaser: The first Japanese Nobel laureate in literature (1968) — his Snow Country (1948), Thousand Cranes and The Old Capital are masterpieces of a prose so delicate it is almost silence. He was an orphan who wrote of beauty and loneliness, and he took his own life in 1972 by gas, leaving no note. The Palm-of-the-Hand Stories, his miniatures, are among the most perfect short works in any language. His influence on modern Japanese prose is total.

exploreAction.targetName: Snow Country — the novel of the mountain resort
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first pages and feel the snow — the novel opens with the train through the tunnel. Kawabata's prose is the finest in modern Japanese, and his love story of the geisha and the dilettante is its purest example.
